items.title: W/Bank mobilises $5.79bn private capital for Nigeria
items.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The World Bank Group has said it is helping to mobilise $5.79 billion in private capital for investment in Nigeria’s agriculture, telecommunications and micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), in a major push to expand private-sector participation in the economy. The financing drive is being supported by policy reforms, investment platforms, risk-sharing mechanisms and commercial financing aimed at removing barriers to investment and unlocking opportunities across critical sectors. The initiative is also expected to strengthen food security, improve access to finance for small businesses, expand digital connectivity and create jobs, as the Federal Government intensifies efforts to improve the business environment and attract private investment. “The World Bank supports reforms and projects that improve the investment environment and create viable opportunities. IFC complements this work by structuring investments, deploying its own capital, and bringing commercial lenders and institutional investors into those opportunities,” the institution said. In agriculture, the World Bank Group highlighted financing arrangements for Dangote Industries Limited fertilizer production and Indorama Fertilizer, which it said were helping to expand domestic fertiliser production and improve access to agricultural inputs for more than 10 million smallholder farmers. According to the institution, IFC helped mobilise $1.02 billion for Dangote through refinancing and financing from development institutions and commercial lenders, while $282.5 million was mobilised for Indorama through syndicated financing. The two projects have a combined production capacity of 6.8 million metric tonnes annually, a development the bank said could reduce Nigeria’s dependence on imported inputs, improve affordability and strengthen food security. $1.89bn for small businesses The World Bank Group said its Fostering Inclusive Finance for MSMEs in Nigeria programme, known as FINCLUDE, was designed to improve the availability and quality of financing for more than 250,000 micro, small and medium enterprises operating in job-intensive sectors. Thirty per cent of the financing is targeted at women-led businesses, reflecting efforts to broaden access to credit among enterprises that often struggle to secure affordable funding. The programme is backed by a $500 million package from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, combining financing and risk-sharing instruments to encourage financial institutions and other investors to extend additional capital to underserved businesses. The bank said FINCLUDE was expected to mobilise nearly $1.89 billion in private financing and support an estimated 850,000 direct and indirect jobs. The initiative is particularly significant for Nigeria, where access to affordable credit remains a major constraint on the ability of small businesses to expand operations, invest in equipment and generate employment. Telecoms attract $1.1bn In the telecommunications sector, IFC acted as an anchor investor in a $1.2 billion bond issuance by IHS Towers, helping to mobilise more than $1.1 billion from private investors and broaden participation in the transaction. The World Bank Group said the transaction demonstrated investor confidence in Nigeria’s digital infrastructure sector and its capital markets. It noted that the tower-sharing model adopted by IHS Towers enables mobile network operators to expand connectivity more quickly and at lower cost while reducing the environmental footprint of network deployment.Beyond telecommunications, the institution said its Building Resilient Digital Infrastructure for Growth (BRIDGE) Project would introduce a new model for developing Nigeria’s digital infrastructure through public-private partnerships. Under the arrangement, a nationwide open-access fibre-optic network will be built, owned and operated through private-sector participation rather than relying exclusively on public financing. The first round of investor selection is expected to mobilise at least $156 million in private equity, while subsequent financing rounds could unlock up to $1.1 billion in private investment by 2030. The project is expected to extend affordable broadband access to an additional 58 million people, increasing coverage from 92 million people in 2025 to 150 million by 2030. Its beneficiaries are projected to include an additional 42 million young people and 15 million women. The project will also connect millions of households, 38,800 public schools, 16,900 health facilities and 3,400 local government offices to high-speed broadband internet. According to the bank, the expanded connectivity would bring digital services closer to communities, improve access to education and healthcare, facilitate public service delivery and create new opportunities for businesses and livelihoods. The World Bank Group attributed the growing opportunities for private capital, in part, to reforms undertaken by the Federal Government to improve foreign exchange management, strengthen public finances, reform fuel subsidies and establish more predictable conditions for investors. items.title: Tinubu writes Senate, forwards 5 bills on drug enforcement, transport, others
items.description: By Henry Umoru President Bola Tinubu has written the Senate, transmitting a series of bills for consideration and the bills include proposed legislation to amend the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Act, establish a National School of Government and reform the legal framework governing the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency, NDLEA, among others. The bills, in accordance with the provisions of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, were conveyed by the President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio. The Executive communications were read on Tuesday by Akpabio. One of the proposals, the Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Amendment Bill 2026, seeks to amend the existing 2022 Act to reposition the bureau as an independent authority and expand its mandate. The proposed amendment also seeks to transfer supervisory oversight of the bureau to the Presidency, alongside changes to its administrative structure. According to the letter, “The Nigerian Safety Investigation Bureau Amendment Bill seeks to reposition the Bureau as an independent multimodal safety investigation authority, expanding its mandate beyond aviation to maritime and other transport occurrences. “It also proposes transferring the Bureau’s oversight to the Presidency and strengthening its institutional, operational, administrative and constitutional framework. Another proposal, the NDLEA Bill 2026, seeks to establish a consolidated legal framework for the operations of the NDLEA. The bill is expected to strengthen the agency’s powers, including its capacity to investigate individuals suspected of involvement in illicit drug-related activities. According to the letter, “The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency Bill seeks to repeal the existing NDLEA Act and the Indian Hemp Act, both contained in the Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. “The proposed legislation is intended to establish a consolidated legal framework for combating the cultivation, processing, trafficking and use of illicit drugs. “It also seeks to empower the agency to investigate persons suspected of involvement in drug-related activities.” President Tinubu also transmitted the National School of Government Bill (ASCON) 2026, which seeks to repeal the Administrative staff college of Nigeria act and establish a National School of Government. The proposed institution is intended to serve as a national centre for governance training, public sector capacity development and institutional strengthening. The National School of Government Bill seeks to repeal the Administrative Staff College of Nigeria Act and establish a new institution to serve as a national centre for leadership development, policy delivery and executive capacity-building. The President equally transmitted a bill seeking to domesticate the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their two Additional Protocols of 1977, which provide for the protection of victims of armed conflict, as well as the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, providing for the enforcement of punishment on genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. The letter reads further, “The Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols Bill seeks to repeal the existing Geneva Conventions Act and give effect in Nigeria to the 1949 Geneva Conventions and the two Additional Protocols adopted in 1977. “The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (Enforcement) Bill seeks to domesticate the Rome Statute and establish a framework for the enforcement and punishment of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and related offences. “It also provides for Nigeria’s cooperation with the International Criminal Court in the performance of its functions”. Akpabio thereafter referred the bills to the Committee on Rules and Business for further legislative action. Meanwhile, the Senate received notification of President Tinubu’s assent to two amendment bills providing for the inclusion of federal universities in Yaba, Lagos, and Kaduna in the relevant laws governing federal universities of technology. Akpabio said the Federal University of Technology Amendment No. 2 Bill, 2026, provides for the inclusion of the Federal University of Technology and Vocational Studies in Yaba in the relevant Act. “The Federal University of Technology Amendment Bill, 2026, seeks to amend the Federal Universities of Technology Act to include the Federal University of Technology and Vocational Studies in Kaduna”. He thereafter referred the documents to the Clerk to the National Assembly for further action. Akpabio commended Tinubu for assenting to the two bills, describing the development as an important step towards promoting education in Nigeria. items.title: NAF Plane Crash: Igbokoda residents lament stench, fear disease outbreak, as body parts float
items.description: By Dayo Johnson, Akure More than a week after a Nigerian Air Force, NAF, aircraft crashed in Igbokoda, Ondo State, residents said they are battling offensive odour, polluted water and fear for disease outbreak. Read Also: NAF PLANE CRASH: How hero pilot died saving town The NAF ATR-42, which was flying from Benin City to Lagos, crashed into a swamp near the Air Force Forward Operating Base in Igbokoda on October 5, killing all 25 persons on board. They appealed to the Federal Government, Ondo State government and the Nigerian Air Force to urgently evacuate the human remains, clean up the environment and provide safe drinking water for the community. The aircraft was on a routine operation when it crashed on Monday, October 5, killing all 25 persons on board, comprising five crew members and 20 passengers. It submerged into the swamp, prompting a joint search and recovery operation by the Air Force, other security agencies and emergency responders. More than a week after, locals say the operation is yet to be fully concluded. Community leaders and residents told Vanguard that the decomposing bodies and spillage of aviation fuel have left the entire area polluted. Body parts float The Olu of Igbokoda, Oba Afolabi Odidiomo, said the stench from the crash site has spread to residential areas, making life unbearable for residents. He said body parts were still seen floating on the river, while traces of fuel could be observed some distance from the wreckage site. “The odour is extremely offensive and unbearable. So many parts of human bodies are floating around in the river. Some of the bodies have not been recovered, they have decomposed and it is affecting everything,” the monarch said. According to him, the development has raised serious concerns over contamination of the river, which serves as a major source of water for domestic use. “People are worried about cooking, bathing and other domestic uses. We are appealing to government to urgently remove the remaining bodies and debris, contain any fuel spillage and carry out full environmental remediation,” Oba Odidiomo said. He also called for immediate provision of potable water for residents pending conclusion of recovery and clean-up operations, stressing that the welfare of the host community should not be overlooked. Smell For residents living near the river, the experience has been distressing. Omogbemi Damola, a resident, said she has been perceiving the foul odour in her upstairs apartment for days. “What happened in Igbokoda is a very sad experience. Since the accident occurred, different kinds of unpleasant odours have been carried by the breeze into our homes. “I live upstairs and I have been perceiving the smell for at least four days now,” she said. She appealed to the state government to expedite action on the recovery of bodies and measures to control the stench, noting that the community has already suffered enough trauma from the incident. Another resident, Oroyo Levy, said the situation has gone beyond discomfort to a public health concern. “We are appealing to government to act swiftly to contain the odour and prevent it from posing further health risks. “The smell suggests air pollution and we are worried about its effect, especially on children,” Levy said. He described the crash as an unusual and painful experience for the riverine community, and urged authorities to investigate the environmental impact of the incident to avert another crisis. Levy added that more than a week after the tragedy, uncertainty over water safety has heightened anxiety among residents who depend on the river. Residents therefore urged the National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA; State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, and relevant environmental agencies to intervene and ensure that the aftermath of the crash does not trigger an outbreak of waterborne diseases. Govt reacts Reacting, the State Commissioner for Environment, Tob Loko, said the state government was collaborating with the Federal Government to ensure maximum recovery. “The state government is collaborating with the Federal Government to ensure that we carry out as much recovery as possible. “But you know that despite the number of days the recovery effort has been ongoing, no meaningful recovery has been made. None of the corpses has been recovered. “Shortly afterwards, concerns about pollution were raised. What we are trying to do is make a holistic assessment of the level of public health impact and determine how we can embark on decontamination efforts because the surrounding area is surely contaminated. “So, there is a case of pollution. But we are not resting on our laurels. As I have said, we are carefully undertaking holistic assessments of the environmental impact and the public health impact of what has happened there to ensure that we address it as quickly as possible,” he said. ‘They have drinking water’ On claims of drinking water pollution, the commissioner said the complaint was not entirely correct. “That is not the water they drink. There are boreholes around. So, the claim that the water is no longer useful is not entirely correct. “Let me also say this: Some people insinuate that the site of the crash is close to the metropolis. Of course, the crash site is at least 500 metres away from the bulk of the metropolis. So, the issue of not having water to drink and other associated concerns is not there. “We are not ruling out the fact that there may be cases of pollution. But to say that the people do not have water to drink as a result of the crash is not a sustainable argument or concern, so to speak,” Loko added. items.title: L’Algérie achète 600 000 tonnes de blé au prix de 326-326,5 $/t
items.description: L’Algérie achète une nouvelle quantité de blé tendre au prix compris entre 362 et 326,5 dollars la tonne en coût et fret (C&F). Un mois après avoir acquis 500 000 tonnes à un prix compris entre 319 et 321 dollars la tonne (C&F), l’Office algérien des céréales (OAIC), a conclu un nouvel achat de 600 000 tonnes de cette céréale, rapporte l’agence Reuters. Le monopole public des importations de céréales ne communique pas sur ses appels d’offres, ni sur les quantités achetées et les pays d’origine. Selon l’agence de presse britannique qui cite des négociants, les 600 000 tonnes de blé tendre achetées par l’Algérie mardi pourraient provenir de Russie, de Roumanie, de Bulgarie et d’Argentine. L’Algérie achète 600 000 tonnes de blé tendre au prix fort Pour les livraisons, elles devraient être effectuées du 1er au 15 décembre et du 16 au 31 décembre. Si le blé est originaire d’Amérique du Sud ou d’Australie, il faut compter un mois de plus. L’Algérie a importé 1,1 million de tonnes de blé dans un contexte où les prix sont les plus élevés sur le marché mondial des céréales, en raison notamment de la crise en mer Noire qui empêche la Russie et l’Ukraine, deux grands producteurs de cette céréale, d’expédier leurs récoltes. Avec 8,5 millions de tonnes à importer durant la campagne 2026-2027, l’Algérie fait partie des trois plus grands importateurs de céréales au monde derrière l’Egypte (13,5 millions de tonnes) et l’Indonésie (12,5 millions de tonnes). Le blé tendre, dont l’Algérie n’est pas un grand producteur, est utilisé pour produire du pain et de la farine, deux produits subventionnés par l’Etat et qui font partie des plus consommés dans le pays. items.title: Nigerians warned against relocating to Indonesia without business plans
items.description: Nigerians seeking greener pastures in Indonesia have been advised to invest in their home country rather than relocate without viable business plans, as employment opportunities for foreigners are limited and setting up businesses requires substantial capital. The Charge d’Affaires ad interim of the Nigerian Embassy in Jakarta, Eze Nduka, gave the advice while speaking to journalists at the embassy on Tuesday. Nduka said many Nigerians had spent between 10 and 15 years in Indonesia without meaningful employment, while some had become stranded and were seeking assistance from the embassy to return home. He urged Nigerian youths to verify claims about opportunities in Indonesia and avoid travelling based on promises made online, particularly those linked to drug trafficking, cybercrime and other criminal activities. According to him, some Nigerians have also spent years in the country without valid immigration documents, restricting their freedom of movement and access to opportunities. He advised prospective migrants to develop clear plans before travelling, including identifying whom they intend to meet, the business they hope to establish and how they would sustain themselves. “Many of them are here, they have spent 10-15 years doing nothing. Some of them are coming to the embassy crying, asking us that they want to go home. They don’t have transportation, that we should find a means of repatriation and all that,” he said. Nduka urged Nigerians to consider the four Ws and other essential questions before relocating, including who they were going to meet, what business they intended to pursue, where and when they would operate, and how they would survive. “The only advice I have for them is this: you must employ those four Ws in everything you are going to do. Who you are coming to meet, what business you are coming to do, and where and when and how you will survive in Indonesia, because there’s no job here in Indonesia, there’s no job for foreigners,” he said. The envoy said establishing a business in Indonesia was expensive, requiring significant financial resources to meet the country’s business and residence requirements. He advised Nigerians with the financial capacity to establish businesses abroad to consider investing at home, where their investments could contribute to economic growth and job creation. “In terms of business, to set up a business here in Indonesia is quite expensive. Even to set up a business, you must have some deposit of millions of naira, so if you are bringing in that money here, why not invest home?” he asked. Nduka also warned Nigerians against engaging in drug trafficking and cybercrime, saying Indonesia had strengthened its cybersecurity systems and enforcement of laws against such offences. He said the country had introduced stricter policies, making it increasingly difficult for offenders to evade law enforcement. “Indonesia has really improved in terms of cybersecurity and other technologies. Before, Indonesia used to be a kind of endpoint that any money you wanted to move out, or that you must have made from any part of the world, you could come here and clear it. “But there are new governments, there are new policies. It’s no longer business as usual. Many of them are still in detention. Many of them are on life sentence. Many of them are on death sentence. Many of them are on long-term prison,” he said. The envoy said the Nigerian population in Indonesia had declined significantly compared with previous decades, partly because of stricter enforcement against drug-related offences and cybercrime. He added that some Nigerians had encountered difficulties accessing vocational training and employment, making it more challenging for them to establish themselves in the country. Nduka, however, encouraged Nigerian investors to explore legitimate business opportunities in Indonesia, describing the country as a market with considerable potential for bilateral trade and investment. He said Indonesian companies had established businesses in Nigeria across several sectors, including manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, oil and gas, petrochemicals, consumer goods and healthcare. Among the Indonesian-linked companies operating in Nigeria, he listed Indorama, Primera Food, Wing Group and Orange Group. The envoy urged Nigerian investors to study Indonesia’s business environment and establish credible partnerships with local companies, noting that previous cases of fraud had undermined Indonesian suppliers’ confidence in Nigerian businesses. He called on Nigerian companies to demonstrate their credibility through verifiable registration documents and transparent business dealings. “Tell our investors that they should utilise this government-to-government trade expo and prove to them that their company is duly registered with the CAC,” he said. On bilateral relations, Nduka said trade between Nigeria and Indonesia had continued to expand, with opportunities for both countries to strengthen cooperation in manufacturing, renewable energy, agriculture, pharmaceuticals and waste management. He encouraged Nigerians attending the trade expo in Indonesia to use the platform to establish genuine business relationships and explore investment opportunities. The envoy also said Nigeria could benefit from studying Indonesia’s approach to infrastructure development, particularly its use of public-private partnerships to finance roads, railways and other major projects. He explained that such arrangements could enable private companies to finance and maintain infrastructure in exchange for revenue generated over an agreed period, thereby reducing the immediate financial burden on government. On the welfare of Nigerians in Indonesia, Nduka disclosed that six Nigerians died in the country between January and August 2026. He said the embassy was working with relevant authorities to establish the circumstances surrounding some of the deaths and provide consular assistance to affected families. According to him, the mission had visited detention facilities, supported burial arrangements, communicated with families in Nigeria and assisted with the repatriation of deceased citizens. He added that the embassy was following up on cases involving Nigerians detained over criminal offences and those requiring assistance to return home. Nduka urged Nigerians in Indonesia to report emergencies and other serious incidents to the embassy promptly to enable the mission to engage the appropriate authorities. He also called for stronger coordination among Nigerian community groups in Indonesia, saying a more unified approach would help the embassy communicate with citizens and address their concerns effectively. items.title: GMTF targets Volta healthcare gaps with equipment, specialist training and patient support
items.description: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is prioritising medical equipment, specialist training and financial support for patients as it works to close gaps in specialised healthcare in the Volta Region. The Fund’s Administrator, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, said improving access to care required a comprehensive approach that combined financial assistance with investment in diagnostic equipment, specialist expertise and effective referral systems. She was speaking at an engagement with medical professionals and healthcare stakeholders in Ho as part of the Fund’s first-anniversary activities and nationwide sensitisation tour. The event, dubbed “One Year On – An Evening of Reflection”, brought together the Volta Regional Minister, James Gunu, medical directors, specialists, other healthcare professionals and representatives of Roche Ghana. Ms Darko-Opoku urged health professionals to identify and document equipment shortages, inadequate diagnostic capacity, referral challenges and gaps in specialist services. She called for evidence-based recommendations to guide the Fund’s interventions and improve patient outcomes. She explained that the GMTF’s four pillars—financial support for eligible patients, medical equipment and infrastructure, specialist training, and research and innovation—were designed to address both treatment costs and the capacity of health facilities to deliver quality care. Speaking on behalf of the Chief Executive Officer of Ho Teaching Hospital, the Medical Director, Dr Emmanuel Kasu, urged the Fund to prioritise the early identification and enrolment of eligible patients, better referral coordination, support to help patients navigate the care process and faster provision of medical equipment. He said the Fund’s impact should be measured beyond patient enrolment to include timely access to treatment, improved clinical outcomes and reduced financial hardship for patients and their families. Reflecting on the Fund’s first year, Ms Darko-Opoku said its patient-support programme began with a pilot involving 50 patients nationwide. The exercise helped management assess procedures, identify implementation challenges and improve systems ahead of expanding assistance. She also highlighted the development of the Fund’s Medicines List and Tariff Manual, prepared with input from specialists and subject-matter experts to guide decisions on eligible treatments, procedures and costs. On infrastructure, she cited the restoration of the Cardiac Catheterisation Laboratory at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital and the development of cardiology centres at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital and Tamale Teaching Hospital. She also highlighted a partnership with KGL Group to support a US$10 million diagnostic and imaging centre at the Greater Accra Regional Hospital. Ms Darko-Opoku stressed that investment in modern equipment must be accompanied by specialist training to ensure its effective use and improve patient outcomes. She acknowledged challenges encountered during patient onboarding and said the GMTF Care digital platform was operational, with ongoing improvements to simplify applications, strengthen communication and reduce delays. She urged healthcare professionals to educate patients about the Fund’s mandate and application procedures, particularly those living far from major urban centres who might otherwise miss out on available support. Ms Darko-Opoku reaffirmed the Fund’s commitment to working with health institutions and other stakeholders to close gaps in specialised healthcare, reduce the financial burden of treatment and improve access to quality care. She commended Mr Gunu for his support and thanked Roche Ghana for sponsoring the engagement.

items.title: Intelligence artificielle | Attention au piège des benchmarks !
items.description: L’Occident s’est enfermé dans une illusion métrologique où chaque semaine, des classements dorés à l’or fin décernent la «suprématie de l’intelligence artificielle» sur la base de benchmarks devenus de véritables pièces de théâtre. On compare des pourcentages d’exactitude sur des tests d’école (MMLU, HumanEval, Math), comme si l’on mesurait la puissance militaire de deux empires en comptant le nombre de médailles obtenues à un concours de tir à l’arc. Mahjoub Lotfi Belhedi * La réalité est bien plus brutale : la caducité des techniques actuelles de benchmarking est quasi-totale. L’évaluation de l’IA ne souffre plus d’un manque de précision, mais d’un biais d’invalidation fondamentale. Les modèles de frontière sont surentraînés pour réussir les tests, ils connaissent les réponses aux examens avant même de s’y présenter. Mais surtout, ces benchmarks mesurent une performance statique, en laboratoire, ignorant la véritable nature de la guerre technologique : la puissance infrastructurelle, l’agilité systémique et surtout l’imprévisibilité stratégique. Déclarer aujourd’hui les États-Unis vainqueur sur la base des benchmarks d’OpenAI ou d’Anthropic est une erreur d’appréciation stratégique. La suprématie de l’IA ne se joue pas dans une feuille de calcul, mais sur le terrain d’une guerre invisible structurée par quatre piliers matériels et surtout une variable x imprévisible. Primo, la guerre des modèles : la brute de la Silicon Valley face à l’alchimie de «Hangzhou». La méthodologie américaine repose sur «le scaling law brutal» qui consiste à injecter plus de paramètres, consommer plus de térawatts, empiler plus de milliards. Les USA produisent des titans monolithiques, ultra-performants sur le papier, mais lourds et extrêmement coûteux à faire tourner. Côté chinois, la contrainte a engendré une mutation techno-génétique. Privée de la force brute par les sanctions, la Chine a développé une culture de l’optimisation extrême. L’épisode DeepSeek n’était qu’un tir de sommation : la démonstration qu’une architecture distribuée, distillée et basée sur un apprentissage par renforcement frugal pouvait égaler les monstres américains pour une fraction ridicule de leur coût. Pendant que Washington évalue la «réflexion» de ses modèles sur des énigmes logiques, Pékin déploie des dizaines de milliers de modèles légers, spécialisés (Agentic AI), directement greffés sur son tissu industriel, son réseau de surveillance et sa robotique. L’un calcule la métaphysique, l’autre orchestre l’économie matérielle. Secundo, les data centers et l’énergie, la faille du réseau américain. Si l’IA est le nouveau cerveau global, les data centers en sont le système nerveux central. Dans ce périmètre stratégique, les benchmarks de laboratoire oublient la physique. Les USA affichent une capacité cumulée impressionnante et des projets pharaoniques (Stargate et clusters de gigawatts), mais ils heurtent un mur imprévu : la vétusté de leur réseau électrique, les blocages bureaucratiques et l’opposition des populations locales face à la surconsommation d’eau et d’électricité. À l’inverse, la Chine aborde la question de la puissance de calcul avec la rigueur d’une planification d’État centralisée. Avec son projet stratégique de «Routage des données de l’Est vers l’Ouest» (East Data, West Computing) lancé officiellement en février 2022, Pékin connecte directement ses mégacentres de calcul aux barrages hydroélectriques du Sud-Ouest et aux immenses parcs solaires et éoliens du désert de Gobi. La Chine ne construit pas juste des serveurs, elle bâtit une infrastructure énergétique dédiée à l’inférence en temps réel. Tertio, les semi-conducteurs : l’embargo américain a-t-il vraiment bloqué la Chine ? En interdisant la vente de ses puces de pointe (comme les Nvidia H100 ou B200…), Washington pensait paralyser l’essor de l’IA en Chine. C’était sans compter sur la résilience et l’agilité d’un pays habitué à innover sous pression. Loin d’être freinée, la Chine a structuré son propre écosystème matériel indépendant. Symbole éclatant de cette riposte : le déploiement massif de puces de dernière génération comme la Huawei Ascend 910C, associée aux superclusters de calcul CloudMatrix. Ces accélérateurs ultrapuissants démontrent la force de la stratégie chinoise du «dépassement en virage» . Pour surmonter l’absence d’équipements de lithographie EUV occidentale, les ingénieurs chinois repensent toute l’architecture microélectronique : – empilement de mini-puces et intégration 3D avancée pour démultiplier les performances sans dépendre des procédés de gravure de TSMC ; – optimisation logicielle poussée (via le Framework Cann de Huawei) et réseaux d’interconnexion optique pour contourner les verrous de mémoire ; – pari sur les technologies de rupture, notamment l’industrialisation des premières puces à lumière (calcul photonique) et des architectures neuromorphiques imitant le cerveau humain. Si les benchmarks d’aujourd’hui ne mesurent que la vitesse d’exécution sur puces occidentales, la Chine a créé en secret un écosystème matériel parallèle. De la conception de puces Asic sur mesure à la maîtrise de l’interconnexion chiplet (un type de micropuce), en passant par l’optimisation logicielle des accélérateurs Huawei (Ascend), les ingénieurs chinois ont appris à faire sauter les verrous d’efficacité. Le goulot d’étranglement de la mémoire HBM et de la lithographie EUV pousse la Chine vers des paradigmes alternatifs : calcul photonique, processeurs analogiques et architectures neuromorphiques. Si une seule de ces voies franchit le seuil de viabilité commerciale, le monopole de l’architecture x86/GPU – issu du mariage entre le processeur central (CPU x86) et le processeur graphique (GPU) – s’effondre du jour au lendemain. Autrement dit, l’embargo américain sur les puces Nvidia (H100, B200) censé paralyser l’IA chinoise n’a pas tenu en compte la capacité d’adaptation d’un pays habitué aux contraintes de siège. Quarto, le système sanguin mondial : les câbles sous-marins & l’Internet physique On oublie souvent que l’IA «dans le cloud» repose sur des câbles de fibre optique sous-marins reposant par 4 000 mètres de fond. La suprématie de l’IA n’est rien sans la maîtrise de sa distribution en millisecondes. Dans cette arène silencieuse, la compétition est féroce. La Chine déploie ses propres dorsales internationales (comme le câble Peace qui s’inscrit directement dans le volet numérique des Nouvelles Routes de la Soie) pour interconnecter le Sud Global (Asie du Sud-Est, Moyen-Orient, Afrique, Amérique Latine) sans passer par les bifurcations américaines ou européennes. En contrôlant les tuyaux par lesquels transitent les modèles open-source chinois distribués massivement, Pékin garantit que la couche applicative mondiale tournera sur ses standards infrastructurels, neutralisant toute tentative de blocage numérique par l'Occident. Quinto, la discrétion Chinoise et le scénario du Jour J. C’est dans ce cadre précis que le benchmarking traditionnel révèle son absurdité totale. Les métriques occidentales ne mesurent que ce qui est rendu public et commercialisé. En Chine, une bonne partie de l’écosystème d’IA est marquée par une lisibilité stratégique fort réduite. Tandis que les entreprises de la Silicon Valley font du bruit médiatique à chaque version mineure pour rassurer leurs investisseurs, les laboratoires chinois (qu’ils soient liés à l’Académie chinoise des sciences, à l’armée ou aux géants de la tech) opèrent sous le sceau du secret opérationnel. Selon les spécialistes en IA, les technologies majeures chinoises en cours d’expérimentation à l’abri des regards touchent, entre autres : – des modèles hybrides alliant Quantum Computing et réseaux de neurones pour la cryptanalyse et la simulation moléculaire ; – des architectures d’IA militaires en mesure d’opérer en essaims autonomes sans connexion réseau ; – des algorithmes de raisonnement synthétique à très faible empreinte mémoire, apte de tourner sur des puces grand public dégradées. Cette tendance de rupture globale démontre que le potentiel d’évolution de la Chine en IA n'est pas linéaire, il est exponentiel et discontinu. Et l’illusion de la suprématie américaine reposant sur un score de 92% à un test standardisé contre 89% pour un modèle chinois est une berceuse pour diplomates. Il suffirait de quelques heures par la publication surprise d’une rupture architecturale, l’activation d’un réseau de puces photoniques souverain ou la mise à disposition globale d’un modèle AGI open-source ultraléger pour que la suprématie bascule instantanément. In fine, pendant que l’Occident pèse des plumes sur des balances électroniques, la Chine est en train de couler une enclume. La vraie suprématie de l’IA ne sera pas proclamée par un classement sur GitHub, elle sera constatée le jour où le monde entier réalisera que l’infrastructure de son économie tourne déjà sur un modèle dont il ne possède pas la clé. * Stratège en réflexion IA. L’article Intelligence artificielle | Attention au piège des benchmarks ! est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: IMF: Nigeria’s banks need stronger safeguards after recapitalisation
items.description: *Flags sovereign debt exposure as banking sector risk *Calls for adequate capital, liquidity buffers, timely recognition of bad loans *Warns AI market correction could trigger wider global financial instability By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor, in Bangkok, Thailand The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged Nigerian authorities to strengthen regulatory safeguards in the banking sector following recapitalisation, warning that “the sovereign and bank nexus is also an important area” of concern for African economies. Read Also: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF •PRESS BRIEFING: From left – Director of the Research Department, Silvana Tenreyro; Deputy Director, Research Department, Petya Koeva-Brooks, and Division Chief, Research Department, Deniz Igan, all of International Monetary Fund, IMF, at the press briefing on the Fund’s World Economic Outlook, WEO, report, released at the ongoing annual meetings of the World Bank/IMF in Bangkok, Thailand. Photo by Babajide Komolafe. Assistant Director, Monetary and Capital Markets Department, IMF, Jason Wu, gave this recommendation at a press briefing on the release of its Global Financial Stability Report, during the ongoing World Bank/IMF annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, stressing that stronger capital bases must be complemented by adequate liquidity requirements, timely recognition of bad loans and effective monitoring of banks’ exposure to government debt to build resilience against financial shocks. Wu said: “What we often see in emerging economies is that, after recapitalisation, there is a need to impose appropriate regulations to prevent risks from building up in the future.” He added: “These include adequate capital and liquidity requirements as well as timely recognition of credit losses and bad loans.” Highlighting the relationship between banks and governments as a critical area requiring closer attention in Africa, Wu said, “In Africa in particular, I think the sovereign, bank nexus is also an important area. So is understanding the exposure to sovereign risks.” He stressed that these measures were essential to strengthening the banking system, stating: “So I think those are critical elements to building further resilience in the banking sector.” Monetary policy outlook Commenting on the recent decision of the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) to reduce its Monetary Policy Rate, MPR, by 350 basis points to 23 per cent, following the three consecutive months decline in the country’s inflation rate to 15.39 per cent in August from 15.93 in May 2026, Wu noted that Nigeria’s improving inflation outlook could create room for a less restrictive stance, while emphasising the need for credible, data-driven decisions by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). “We have seen improvements on the inflation front, which suggests that perhaps a not-as-tight monetary policy stance would be appropriate,” Wu stated, stressing that the CBN must sustain confidence in its policy decisions. “I think what’s important is credibility. The central bank has to be data-driven and has to be able to explain the decisions clearly. So far, based on what we have seen, it seems like the news is on the good front,” he said. Wu further emphasised the importance of communication in managing inflation, saying: “Further data dependence, clear, transparent monetary policy communications give a key to containing this wave of inflation shocks.” AI boom poses global financial risks Beyond Nigeria, the IMF, in its Global Financial Stability, GFS Report, warned that the growing concentration of investments in artificial intelligence (AI), coupled with ambitious earnings expectations, could expose global financial markets to a potentially destabilising correction. The GFS report, among other things, highlighted financing arrangements involving AI companies, including equity investments, debt and commitments linked to future revenues. Explaining the findings from the report, Deputy Director, Monetary and Capital Markets Department, IMF, Athanasios Vamvakidisan, said: “We looked at 14 public transactions and what we found is about $300 billion in equity investments and $650 billion in debt investments.” Vamvakidisan explained that the transactions involved “$1.4 trillion of future revenue commitments,” adding that the future revenue component made the arrangements unusual. He warned that the structure could amplify losses if AI companies failed to deliver expected returns. “If there are questions about the monetisation in AI, the equity investments will deplete the value, the debt may be difficult to service and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialise,” he said. The GFS report also questioned whether the strong earnings performance that has supported market optimism could continue indefinitely. “In recent quarters, the actual earnings beat these expectations and the market upgraded the forecast even higher,” Vamvakidisan said, describing a cycle in which positive earnings surprises fuel increasingly ambitious expectations. He warned that sustaining the trend could become more difficult as expectations rise and market exposures become concentrated. Vanguard News The post IMF: Nigeria’s banks need stronger safeguards after recapitalisation appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: HOCKEY: HOPE AND REALITY
items.description: Pakistan’s hockey team won the bronze medal at the 2026 Asian Games. Is this satisfactory or unsatisfactory? The answer to this is not straightforward. A medal is always welcome. Pakistan failed to win a medal at the previous two Asian Games. Yet, for a country with an enviable Asian Games record of eight gold medals — compared to India’s five — a bronze hardly represents a return to the top. There is another, more important, way of looking at it. The Asian Games winner earns direct qualification for the 2028 Olympics. Pakistan has missed that opportunity and will now have to negotiate the Olympic qualifying process in early 2028. Sixteen teams will compete in two eight-team tournaments for four or five Olympic berths. That is a daunting prospect for a country that has failed to qualify for the last three Olympics. So, purely in terms of results, there appears to have been little progress. But results alone do not tell the whole story. Pakistan’s hockey team managed to snag a bronze at the recently concluded Asian Games. What does it tell us about the trajectory of Pakistan Hockey? ASIAN GAMES ASSESSED Pakistan began the Asian Games ranked third in Asia and 14th in the world, behind India, which is ranked eighth in the world and Malaysia, ranked 12th. In its pool games, Pakistan had a comfortable passage against the lower-ranked sides, beating Thailand 9-0, Uzbekistan 5-1, China 3-0 and Oman 7-2. Malaysia was the only genuinely testing opponent. It was a pulsating contest, with the lead changing hands repeatedly. Pakistan led 4-3 with only four minutes remaining and, on the run of play, deserved to win. All four Pakistani goals came from penalty corners. Pakistan earned eight penalty corners; Malaysia had only three but converted all of them. Malaysia created only four or five clear chances from open play and scored twice. Pakistan, meanwhile, dominated the third and fourth quarters — apart from the final four minutes — but squandered several opportunities, including some sitters. The contest eventually ended with Malaysia edging Pakistan 5-4. That defeat forced Pakistan into a semi-final against India, the overwhelming favourites and the Pool B winners. Pakistan have not beaten their traditional rivals for more than a decade, and recent encounters have frequently produced one-sided scorelines. Once India surged into a 3-0 lead, it seemed that history was about to repeat itself. But then Pakistan came alive. Captain Abu Bakar Mahmood reduced the deficit with a penalty-corner conversion at the stroke of half-time. The match was transformed in the 45th minute, when an electric move down the right flank ended with Abdul Hannan Shahid finding the net. Soon it was 3-3. Rana Waheed completed another superb attacking move from the right to take Pakistan level. What followed was a thrilling, end-to-end contest, with chances at both ends. Then came the cruelest of endings. India’s winner arrived in the final minute, in bizarre circumstances. Abhishek’s attempted pass was deflected into the Pakistan goal by a Pakistani stick, turning what had seemed an amazing Pakistani recovery into another defeat. The bronze-medal playoff provided another comeback. South Korea led 3-1, but Pakistan recovered to win 5-3. There is a pattern here. Pakistan’s ability to fight back after falling behind has become one of the more encouraging features of the present team. As in the World Cup, the players repeatedly showed that they could recover from two or even three-goal deficits. Even when they could not turn those comebacks into victories or draws, they often transformed apparently lost contests into competitive matches. But the frequency with which Pakistan has to recover from poor starts is also a serious weakness. Why does this team so often concede early goals? Is it tactical? Is it psychological? Is it a problem with game management? The questions require serious technical analysis. But there are other positives. Sufyan Khan is developing into a world-class drag-flicker. His 12 goals made him the joint leading scorer at the Asian Games. Yet Pakistan’s use of its penalty corners against India raises questions. The team earned seven penalty corners but converted only one. Against Oman, three of Pakistan’s penalty-corner goals had come through a two-touch variation. Curiously, that indirect option was not employed against India. There is no shortage of individual talent. Hannan Shahid and Rana Waheed have established themselves as genuinely world-class forwards. Goalkeeper Ali Raza also produced an impressive performance. Captain Abu Bakar is a dependable defender who has the added value of scoring from penalty corners, and his recent signing for Melbourne Cobras in Hockey One — Australia’s premier domestic competition — is another indication of his growing stature. Meanwhile, Abdul Rahman’s goal against Wales at the 2026 FIH World Cup won him the Poligrass Magic Skill Award, selected by fans for the moments that best captured the magic of hockey. So, even during one of the darkest periods in Pakistan hockey’s history, individual talent remains available. Pakistan’s great teams have traditionally possessed a potent weapon: attacks from the right wing. The opponent’s left side is generally regarded as the more vulnerable defensive flank, making the right-wing route particularly effective. Pakistan’s second-half fightback against India provided a vivid demonstration. Both goals that brought Pakistan level originated from superb attacking movements down the right. The lesson is obvious: strengths must be identified, developed and repeatedly exploited. At the other end of the pitch, however, Pakistan continues to commit too many unforced errors. Mistimed tackles and poor clearances in deep defence gave away penalty corners and, on occasions, resulted in soft goals. The team management must address these deficiencies. The broader picture is also worth considering. The Olympics, the World Cup, the Asian Games, the Asia Cup and the Commonwealth Games are the sport’s principal title tournaments. In these competitions, positions matter. Pakistan did not achieve the desired finish in either of the two title events of 2026 — the World Cup and the Asian Games. Given Pakistan hockey’s decline over more than a decade, this was hardly unexpected. But what matters now is whether the current upward trend can be converted into sustained progress. There is no title tournament before the 2028 Olympics. That should simplify Pakistan Hockey’s priorities. From now until the Olympic qualifiers, virtually every major effort should be directed towards building a team capable of qualifying for Los Angeles. The performance graph does appear to be moving upwards. Pakistan went toe-to-toe with India despite the considerable difference in world rankings and a decade of adverse results. That should provide the players with a substantial psychological boost. But there is still a sizeable gap before Pakistan can seriously challenge the world’s top six. One indication of that gap was the difference in tempo between the 2026 World Cup and the Asian Games. The World Cup’s final and semi-finals were played at a frantic pace. The intensity and tempo at the Asian Games were nowhere near that level. Pakistan must bridge that gap. The next step should be extensive and meaningful international exposure. The PHF should seek matches against teams such as New Zealand, France and Ireland, ranked around ninth to 11th in the world. Matches against opponents of that calibre would provide a much more accurate measurement of Pakistan’s progress than victories over lower-ranked Asian sides. The objective should not merely be to play more international hockey. It should be to play the right opponents, under demanding conditions, and to learn how to compete for 60 minutes at the highest tempo. The bronze medal in the Asian Games is, therefore, neither a failure nor a triumph. Pakistan have demonstrated resilience, individual quality and flashes of the attacking hockey that once made them feared across the world. But they still concede too early, make too many defensive errors and struggle to maintain the intensity required against the very best teams. The Olympic qualifiers will tell us whether Pakistan has actually moved forward. For now, the most urgent question remains unanswered: why does a team with the ability to come back from the brink so often put itself there in the first place? The writer is a freelance sports journalist based in Lahore. X: @IjazChaudhry1 Email: ijaz62@hotmail.com Published in Dawn, EOS, October 11th, 2026

items.title: G-24: Nigeria, other developing nations need cheaper financing — Oyedele
items.description: By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor, in Bangkok, Thailand The Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four on International Monetary Affairs and Development, G-24, has called for improved financing conditions, faster debt restructuring and stronger international financial cooperation to support Nigeria and other developing economies facing mounting debt and development financing challenges. Read Also: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF Nigeria’s Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, who is Chairman of the Intergovernmental Group of Twenty-Four on International Monetary Affairs and Development, G-24, made the call at a press conference on the outcome of the meeting of the Group, during the ongoing International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. He said developing countries needed a more responsive international financial system capable of addressing their economic vulnerabilities, supporting growth and ensuring that debt obligations did not undermine development priorities. “Debt vulnerability is a major obstacle to growth in many developing countries,” Oyedele said, highlighting the need for predictable and coordinated approaches to resolving sovereign debt problems. “We call for predictable, timely and coordinated sovereign debt treatments,” he said, stressing the importance of cooperation between creditors and debtors in resolving debt difficulties. The G-24 chairman said the growing financing challenges confronting developing economies required collective action by governments, multilateral development institutions and other international stakeholders. His position reflects concerns that high borrowing costs and debt-service obligations are limiting the fiscal space available to developing countries to finance infrastructure, healthcare, education and other development priorities. Oyedele said the international community must also strengthen the voice and representation of developing economies, particularly vulnerable countries, in global financial institutions. He called for reforms that would make the international financial architecture more responsive to the changing structure of the global economy and the needs of developing countries. “We emphasised the importance of strengthening the voice and representation of developing countries, particularly the most vulnerable economies, in international financial institutions,” he said. According to him, a more representative multilateral system is essential to restoring confidence in the global economy and ensuring that international economic decisions take account of the circumstances of developing nations. “Restoring confidence in the global economy requires a multilateral system grounded in respect for national sovereignty and the principles of the United Nations Charter,” he said. Climate financing Oyedele also called for increased climate financing for developing countries, arguing that efforts to address climate change must take account of the economic and social challenges facing vulnerable populations. He said climate action should not undermine the livelihoods of people in developing countries, particularly those struggling with poverty, food insecurity and inadequate access to essential services. The G-24 chairman stressed the importance of international cooperation in mobilising the resources required to support climate adaptation and sustainable development. “We also stressed the importance of expanding access to climate finance, guided by the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities,” he said. He urged multilateral development banks and other stakeholders to meet their financing commitments. “We expect the World Bank Group, multilateral development banks and other stakeholders to deliver on the target of mobilising at least $300 billion annually by 2035, as established at COP29,” Oyedele said. He also called for international tax reforms to address tax avoidance, profit shifting and illicit financial flows, which reduce the resources available to governments for development. “On international taxation, we called for reforms to address profit shifting, tax avoidance and illicit financial flows,” he said. Oyedele welcomed progress under the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)/G20 Inclusive Framework. Growth must create jobs Director of the G-24 Secretariat, Iyabo Masha, said economic growth must translate into jobs, better living standards and improved opportunities for citizens rather than being measured solely by macroeconomic indicators. “The objective is to create a more liveable environment for our people, irrespective of their circumstances,” Masha said. She stressed that growth must be inclusive and provide tangible benefits for households, particularly young people seeking employment and economic opportunities. “Economic growth must create jobs, provide opportunities for young people and improve living standards,” she said. Masha added that the quality of growth was as important as the pace of expansion. “Growth should be inclusive and translate into tangible benefits for households,” she said. Oyedele, however, emphasised that macroeconomic stability remained a necessary foundation for achieving these development objectives. “Macroeconomic stability is not a bad policy objective. It is actually the foundation of economic growth,” he said. “If a country does not have a stable macroeconomic environment, it becomes difficult to implement structural reforms, employment-generating policies, infrastructure development and other measures needed to support growth,” he added. According to him, macroeconomic stability should complement policies designed to promote productive investment, employment and inclusive development. “The ultimate objective is to ensure that economic growth improves the living standards of our people,” he said. The G-24 also called for reforms to the IMF quota system to reflect changes in the global economy and improve developing countries’ representation in the institution’s decision-making processes. The group argued that the quota framework should recognise the growing importance of emerging markets and developing economies while protecting the interests of smaller and poorer members. It also stressed the need for stronger coordination among creditors, greater transparency in sovereign debt negotiations and more effective participation by private creditors in debt restructuring. The G-24 said these measures would help improve the international debt resolution framework, reduce prolonged uncertainty for countries facing debt distress and create better conditions for sustainable economic growth. Oyedele said restoring confidence in the global economy would require a multilateral system that respects national sovereignty while responding more effectively to the financing and development needs of vulnerable economies. items.title: Telecel Ghana wins 2 awards at the CCIFG Gala and Awards 2026
items.description: Telecel Ghana has been recognised for its commitment to innovation and responsible business, securing two of six major honours at the Chamber of Commerce and Industry France-Ghana (CCIFG) Awards 2026: Digital Transformation & Innovation Excellence and Sustainability & ESG Impact. Organised by the CCIFG, the awards celebrate organisations that demonstrate exceptional business leadership, innovation and impact. The 2026 awards attracted nominations from leading businesses across multiple sectors, all of which were evaluated by an independent multi-sectoral jury comprising industry leaders, consultants and diplomats. Entries underwent a detailed review and validation process, with submissions assessed against clearly defined benchmarks to determine the most deserving winners. The transparency and depth of the evaluation underscore the significance of Telecel Ghana’s victory in two highly contested categories. The event brought together key stakeholders from Ghana’s business community and was attended by distinguished guests including the French Ambassador to Ghana, Her Excellency Diarra Dime-Labille; the Economic Adviser to the President of Ghana and former Finance Minister, Seth Terkper; and the President of the Board of CCI France Ghana, Guillaume Valence. Telecel Ghana’s recognition in the Digital Transformation & Innovation Excellence category reflects the company’s strategic investment in technology solutions that are transforming the experiences of customers, businesses and communities. Over the past year, Telecel has accelerated its digital agenda by building an integrated ecosystem that extends beyond traditional connectivity to enable secure digital transactions, e-commerce, customer engagement, and financial inclusion. Equally significant was Telecel Ghana’s win in the Sustainability & ESG Impact category, recognising its commitment to creating long-term value through environmental stewardship, social impact and strong governance practices. The award acknowledges Telecel’s conviction that business growth must be accompanied by responsible action that benefits communities and contributes to national development. Telecel has embedded ESG principles into both its operations and corporate culture. On the environmental front, the company has planted 43,000 trees over the past five years and expanded its use of renewable energy through 16 solar-powered network exchanges nationwide, helping reduce its environmental footprint while improving operational efficiency. Through the Telecel Ghana Foundation’s Connected for Good agenda, the company has continued to invest in education, digital inclusion, STEM development, and health and community empowerment programmes, positively impacting more than 6,000 beneficiaries in the year under review. Internally, Telecel has championed diversity and inclusion through strong female representation and initiatives that support financial and digital literacy among women entrepreneurs. These efforts are complemented by a governance framework that emphasises ethical business conduct, transparency, regulatory compliance, data protection and accountability. Winning both awards demonstrates that innovation and sustainability are not separate ambitions for Telecel Ghana, but complementary pillars of its business strategy. The recognition affirms the company’s ability to deliver commercially impactful solutions while simultaneously making meaningful contributions to society and the environment. It also serves as a validation of the investments, partnerships and long-term initiatives that continue to position Telecel as a responsible technology leader in Ghana’s digital economy. Komla Buami, External Affairs Director, speaking on what the recognition means to the business, shared that “These awards are a strong endorsement of the work Telecel Ghana is doing to drive meaningful digital transformation while creating lasting value for society. “They recognise the passion, commitment and purpose behind initiatives that expand financial inclusion, strengthen digital access, support communities and advance sustainability. We are honoured by these awards, which reinforce our belief that innovation and responsible business must go hand in hand.”

items.title: Nigeria’s private capital inflows hit $6bn as reforms gather pace — W/Bank
items.description: •Tax-to-GDP ratio rises to 12.5% from 7% — Oyedele By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief Nigeria’s private capital inflows have surged nearly 20-fold to almost $6 billion in 2026 from about $300 million in 2023, President of the World Bank Group, Mr. Ajay Banga, has said, just as the Federal Government (FG) said it has intensified efforts to translate economic reforms into faster growth, job creation and improved living standards. Banga spoke on Monday during a meeting with the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr. Taiwo Oyedele, and the Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, Mr. Olayemi Cardoso, on the sidelines of the 2026 International Monetary Fund, IMF, and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The meeting reviewed Nigeria’s progress in implementing economic reforms and explored strategies to move the economy from macroeconomic stability to sustained growth, increased private investment and stronger domestic revenue generation. According to a statement, yesterday, by Efe Oviakporie, Head of Information and Public relations of the Federal Ministry of Finance, Banga highlighted the significant increase in private capital inflows as evidence of growing investor interest in the Nigerian economy. Oyedele, in his remarks, disclosed that Nigeria’s tax-to-Gross Domestic Product, GDP, ratio had risen from about seven per cent to 12.5 per cent over the same period, strengthening the government’s capacity to finance public investment without resorting to deficit monetisation. The development comes as the FG seeks to consolidate the gains of its economic reforms and create the conditions for increased investment in productive sectors of the economy. According to the Minister, improved domestic revenue mobilisation would provide greater fiscal space for the government to fund critical infrastructure and development priorities. The discussions also focused on how Nigeria could make greater use of World Bank guarantee instruments to unlock financing for infrastructure projects and attract additional private capital into the domestic economy. Such guarantees could help mobilise funding for projects that might otherwise struggle to attract investors, while reducing some of the risks associated with long-term infrastructure investments. Power infrastructure and human capital development were identified as key priorities for sustained public investment, given their implications for business competitiveness, productivity and employment generation. items.title: LCCI proposes 20% petrol price cut in 6-month programme
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI) has proposed a six-month petrol price reduction programme targeting a 15 to 20 per cent cut in pump prices to ease the burden of high energy and transportation costs on Nigerian businesses and households. In a statement, Director-General of LCCI, Dr. Chinyere Almona, said the Federal Government should work with domestic refiners, petroleum marketers, regulators and other stakeholders to achieve progressive, measurable and sustainable reductions in petrol prices. Almona, while commending the Federal Government’s proposed petrol price-stabilisation mechanism, said the initiative was timely, given the pressure of rising energy and transportation costs on business operations, household purchasing power and the competitiveness of Nigerian enterprises. LCCI welcomed the proposed ceiling of N1,350 per litre on the ex-gantry or landing cost of petrol, subject to monthly reviews and public disclosure, describing it as recognition of the economic consequences of excessive volatility in energy prices. However, Almona warned that stabilising petrol prices at elevated levels would not provide sufficient relief to businesses already grappling with high electricity tariffs, alternative power costs, expensive financing and rising logistics expenses. She said the proposed mechanism could cushion businesses against sudden price increases but would not necessarily guarantee reductions in pump prices. According to her, the government should assess the initiative not only by its ability to moderate price volatility but also by its capacity to lower operating costs and improve economic welfare. The LCCI chief also cautioned that requiring refiners and importers to absorb temporary cost increases and recover them when market conditions improve could create deferred obligations that might eventually push prices upwards if not transparently managed. To support the proposed six-month programme, the Chamber recommended that the government ensure predictable and commercially viable crude oil supplies to domestic refineries to reduce procurement uncertainties, foreign exchange exposure and avoidable logistics costs. items.title: Nigerians still suffer high cost of living, despite economic growth — IMF
items.description: *Advocates cash transfers to cushion hardship in Nigeria *Urges FG to cut debt without worsening hardship IMF upgrades forecast for Nigeria’s economic growth to 4.2% *Warns of tougher times as global growth slows to 3.1% *Says AI boom, energy shocks threaten global economic outlook By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said that despite Nigeria’s economic growth and status as an energy exporter, the cost of living remained high, leaving many Nigerians struggling to meet their basic needs. The fund advocated targeted cash transfers and temporary income support for vulnerable households in Nigeria to cushion the impact of high living costs, reduce poverty and improve food security. The IMF, also warned of tougher times as global growth slows to 3.1%, even as it upgraded its forecast for Nigeria’s economic growth for 2026 to 4.2 per cent but warned that rising energy and food prices, geopolitical tensions and potential market corrections linked to artificial intelligence (AI) threaten the global economic outlook. The new forecast was contained in the IMF World Economic Outlook report October 2026, titled Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices,” released yesterday during the ongoing annual meetings of the IMF/World Bank in Bangkok, Thailand. Furthermore, the new forecast represents a one percentage points above the 4.1 per cent, earlier projects by the IMF in the July 2026 edition of its WEO. According to the IMF, “Growth in sub-Saharan Africa is expected to remain stable at 4.5 percent in 2026, though this masks substantial divergence across countries, reflecting differences in policy space, reform implementation, commodity exposure, climate shocks, and access to external financing. “Oil-importing, non-resource-intensive economies are more adversely affected by higher energy and food prices, whereas some larger economies continue to benefit from earlier stabilization and reform efforts, even though they are largely absent from the AI-driven global technology upswing and face headwinds from declines in official development assistance. “Nigeria is supported by improved macroeconomic stability and favorable terms-of-trade effects, though higher prices for essentials are expected to further aggravate poverty and food insecurity.” Global growth under pressure However, the IMF warned that the global economy’s resilience was under increasing pressure, with growth projected to slow from 3.5 per cent in 2025 to 3.1 per cent in 2026, before recovering to 3.4 per cent in 2027. Speaking at the press briefing on the WEO report Sylvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s Economic Counsellor and Director of the Research Department, said: “The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside.” She added: “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding,” stressing the need to restore fiscal space, strengthen supply-side resilience and improve countries’ capacity to withstand future economic shocks. Explaining the global outlook, Tenreyro identified energy and commodity price increases as major factors weighing on economic activity, while investment associated with artificial intelligence had provided support for growth.” The IMF report noted that the global economy had withstood repeated shocks, including geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions, but cautioned that “these margins of adjustment are not unlimited.” According to the IMF, the interaction between geopolitical tensions and technological investment has created divergent growth outcomes across countries. While economies benefiting from technology-related investment and favourable commodity trade conditions have received some support, others face higher import bills, exchange-rate pressures and weaker real incomes. The Fund warned that prolonged geopolitical tensions could keep energy and food prices elevated, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on economic growth. Global headline inflation is projected to rise from 4.1 per cent in 2025 to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, with higher energy and food prices driving the temporary increase. AI boom raises fresh risks The IMF also cautioned that the technology investment boom, particularly in artificial intelligence, could become a source of financial instability. Although AI-related investment has supported economic activity and international trade, the Fund warned that investment gains were concentrated in a relatively small number of firms, sectors and economies. It cautioned that “a reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions.” Such a correction, the report said, could spill over into economies integrated into technology supply chains and markets with significant exposure to technology stocks. Urges fiscal discipline Against this backdrop, Tenreyro called on governments to rebuild fiscal buffers, safeguard financial stability and strengthen private-sector dynamism. “Fiscal policy must be restrained and help contain demand pressures at a time of heightened inflationary risks,” the IMF chief economist said in the report. The Fund also stressed the importance of monetary policy focused on price stability, adding that “central bank independence is instrumental in achieving that goal.” Advocates cash transfers to cushion hardship in Nigeria The Fund advocated targeted cash transfers and temporary income support for vulnerable households in Nigeria to cushion the impact of high living costs, reduce poverty and improve food security. The Fund said the intervention should be accompanied by improved public expenditure quality and stronger revenue collection to help the Federal Government achieve fiscal consolidation and put public debt on a sustainable downward path without worsening the hardship faced by ordinary Nigerians. Chief of the IMF Research Department’s World Economic Studies Division, Deniz Igan, stated this during a press briefing on the Fund’s World Economic Outlook at the ongoing IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Thailand. Igan said that despite Nigeria’s economic growth and status as an energy exporter, the cost of living remained high, leaving many Nigerians struggling to meet their basic needs. “Although economic growth has held up in Nigeria, given that it is an energy exporter, living costs are still very high, and we are very mindful that the population is suffering,” she said. She noted that the pressures were particularly severe because of the rising cost of essential goods, especially food and energy, which account for a significant proportion of household consumption. “In our chapter on fiscal policy, we also examine the pressures countries are facing from the rising cost of living, particularly increases in the prices of essential goods, which account for a significant proportion of the consumption basket,” Igan said. Against this backdrop, she said the IMF was advocating targeted and temporary support for the most vulnerable households to cushion the impact of risingprices. “In this environment, we advocate cash transfers and targeted, temporary income support for the most vulnerable households in Nigeria,” she said. According to her, the intervention would help address the immediate effects of economic hardship on poor households. “Such transfers can help reduce poverty and improve food security,” she said. However, Igan stressed that social protection measures must be accompanied by fiscal reforms to ensure that governments can sustainably finance public spending and gradually reduce their debt burden. “This should be accompanied by a credible medium-term fiscal framework. That framework should focus on improving the quality of public expenditure and strengthening revenue collection,” she said. Responding to the broader policy challenge, specifically how fiscal and monetary policies could be better positioned to ensure that the burden of economic stabilisation did not fall disproportionately on ordinary citizens while preserving price stability and investor confidence, Igan explained that monetary authorities must also balance the need to control inflation against the effects of policy measures on economic activity, particularly when economies face supply-side shocks. On how central banks should respond to an oil price shock that pushes up inflation without a corresponding increase in demand, she said: “This is a classic case of a policy trade-off. Inflation is high, but economic activity is being constrained or reduced by the shock. This is where the central bank needs to manage the trade-off.” She explained that such a situation differs from one in which inflation is driven by strong demand, requiring policymakers to consider the underlying causes of price increases before deciding on the appropriate response. “This is a different situation from what we see in economies experiencing a demand-driven shock,” she said. Central banks’ focus According to Igan, central banks must nevertheless maintain their focus on price stability and ensure that inflation returns to target within the policy horizon. “It must ensure that inflation returns to target within the policy horizon, which we typically consider to be two to three years,” she said. She added that monetary policy should remain sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to target, while policymakers take account of the implications for economic activity. “In such circumstances, the central bank must continue to focus on price stability and ensure that its monetary policy stance remains sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back to target, while also taking account of the effects on economic activity,” Igan said. She noted that the appropriate policy response would depend on the nature of the shock and the circumstances of each economy, including labour-market conditions, the initial level of inflation and the economy’s exposure to the shock. For Nigeria, the IMF’s recommendations underscore the need to combine measures to restore fiscal sustainability and maintain price stability with targeted interventions to protect vulnerable households from rising living costs. The approach, as outlined by Igan, would require improved public spending efficiency, stronger revenue mobilisation and temporary income support for households most affected by economic pressures.
