items.title: India shuts down iconic Delhi protest site after three decades
items.description: For more than three decades, a stretch of road in central New Delhi was where Indians came to be heard, staging rallies to press their demands and hold those in power accountable. Trade unions, retired soldiers, anti-corruption campaigners, women’s rights groups and student activists all protested beside the capital’s iconic 18th-century Jantar Mantar observatory, drawn by its location near the city’s commercial heart and the seat of political power. But this week, the country’s most recognisable stage for public dissent officially lost its status as an authorised protest venue, prompting concerns among activists over shrinking democratic space. “Jantar Mantar as a protest venue has been de-notified,” Delhi Police said in an order issued Monday. Police detain All India party supporters during a protest demanding the resignation of the country’s Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in Ahmedabad on October 13, 2026. —AFP The move comes days after a confrontation between authorities and anti-government protesters led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) online movement. The youth-led group has mobilised thousands to take to the streets over a revision to electoral rolls that critics say could disenfranchise eligible voters, months after separate protests over exam irregularities forced the education minister to resign. While authorities have designated three alternative demonstration venues in Delhi, campaigners say visibility and proximity to lawmakers are central to the right to protest in the world’s largest democracy. “Jantar Mantar is in the centre of the town, it is connected, it is next to parliament… it was a very important space for all protests,” human rights activist Shabnam Hashmi told AFP. “This is nothing but a move to curb dissent.” ‘Spirit of resistance’ Jantar Mantar, meaning an instrument to calculate in Sanskrit, is designed for the observation of astronomical positions with the naked eye. The roughly 1.6-kilometre (one-mile) street next to Jantar Mantar became synonymous with protest after being designated a demonstration site in 1993. In July, thousands of students led by the “cockroach” movement gathered there before attempting to march towards parliament over irregularities in competitive examinations. Security personnel try to prevent detained protesters from escaping from a bus during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 13, 2026.—AFP For nearly a month, Jantar Mantar transformed into a vibrant hub of Gen-Z dissent , its walls transformed into canvases for angry slogans, defiant messages and graffiti challenging the government. Tensions resurfaced this month when police denied permission for a CJP protest at the site demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner over the contentious voter roll revision. On Wednesday, two of CJP’s top leaders, who clambered over the barricades to “reclaim Jantar Mantar” a day before, were sent to jail for five days for alleged trespassing. “Jantar Mantar is not just a location but a spirit of resistance that nobody can ever take away,” the group’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, said. Delhi Police on Tuesday defended their move, citing a directive from the Supreme Court that “suitable alternative sites” for protest “need to be identified and designated”. The developments have reignited debate over where citizens can now take their grievances. Activist Hashmi said protests at Jantar Mantar had already become increasingly restricted in recent years through limits on space and timings. But its location, she said, made it uniquely effective because demonstrators could easily reach parliament, government ministries and media houses. “In a democracy, you require spaces where you can protest,” she said. “This is absolutely unacceptable.” Neighbours complain Authorities have said demonstrations can be held at two venues on the capital’s outskirts, while a third site closer to the centre, Ramlila Maidan, remains available for larger gatherings. But activists argue that moving protests away from the city centre risks reducing turnout and visibility, particularly for campaigners travelling from distant states. Greater transport costs, longer journeys and reduced media attention could all diminish the impact of demonstrations, they say. Some of those living in the Jantar Mantar neighbourhood, however, welcomed the police order. Security personnel try to prevent detained protesters from escaping from a bus during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, October 13, 2026.—AFP “Roads leading to our homes are barricaded, there is noise and garbage, and our daily lives are disrupted,” Varun Seth, a resident, told the Hindustan Times newspaper. Former Delhi Police commissioner Kiran Bedi also defended the move, saying Jantar Mantar’s “sensitive” location made it poorly suited to hosting protests. “Every city does require an open space for democratic expression… but forgets to provide for (it),” she said on social media. A protester told AFP on Tuesday that demonstrators would continue to gather at Jantar Mantar despite the police order. “With great resolve, we will carry out civil disobedience,” she said. “We will sit here and protest,” she added, before being whisked away by police as she attempted to march towards the site.

items.title: What we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer operation
items.description: Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour surgically removed from his right lung on Tuesday in a 90-minute operation described as “ successful ” by the Vatican. Here are what several medical experts told AFP about the surgery and diagnosis. What is pulmonary adenocarcinoma? Pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the type of tumour removed from the Pope, generally comes from “a primary cancer,” said Dr. Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association. She told AFP that “is a good thing” because it means the tumour is from lung cancer instead of generating from the spread of another cancer. There are two main types of lung cancer: “small cell” cancers, which spread aggressively and make up about 10 to 15 per cent of diagnoses, and “non-small cell” cancers, which make up the vast majority. “Adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of what’s called non-small cell lung cancer,” David Spigel, a medical oncologist specialising in lung cancer research at Nashville’s Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told AFP . Promising outlook David Carbone, director of the Oncology Center at Ohio State University, noted that while smoking is the most well-known risk factor for a lung cancer diagnosis, “most lung cancers that we diagnose today are in people who haven’t smoked, or (stopped) many years ago.” Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO), but the prognosis can vary significantly depending on the type of lung cancer and how advanced it is when first detected. “When we look at five-year survival rate from lung adenocarcinoma, and it’s nicely localised, the rate is approximately 63 to 67pc,” Mora said. “But if we catch it early, it becomes 80 to 98pc, especially after surgical removal.” In such a case, the patient “will achieve a cure and never have their life threatened by cancer,” Spigel added. A standard procedure Pope Leo XIV announced the presence of the lung nodule on Sunday, saying it had been “detected at a very early stage” and was localised. The Vatican said “the lower lobe of the right lung was removed” during Tuesday’s operation to remove the mass. “He had part of his right lung taken out, which is the standard procedure,” Carbone told AFP . “There’s a lot of reserve in the lung, and people can have an entire lung removed and live a normal life,” he added. “I would expect that he’d be back to completely full level of activity very soon.” What now? The question now is whether Pope Leo XIV will need additional treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation. According to the experts consulted by AFP , the answer will depend on several factors, such as the size of the cancerous mass removed, how aggressive it was, its genetic characteristics, and whether or not it has spread. A Vatican source indicated that additional testing is underway. For Carbone, the fact that the Pope has already undergone surgery is encouraging. “Because if it had spread to, for example, the lymph nodes in the centre of the chest, he would have had some treatment before surgery, which he didn’t have,” he explained. “They really do go straight to surgery only for the earliest stage tumours, which makes me think this was a very early stage tumour, and has a quite good prognosis.” He stressed that treatment for lung cancer has improved considerably over the past few decades, “and the prognosis is better than ever. So I would be hopeful for a full recovery”.

items.title: Petrol, diesel prices set to fall from Oct. 16 as LPG faces 18.5% hike
items.description: Petrol and diesel prices are expected to fall marginally at the pumps from Friday, October 16, 2026, while liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) could see an 18.5% increase per kilogram. This is according to the Chamber of Oil Marketing Companies’ pricing outlook for the next pricing window. Breakdown Petrol is projected to decline by almost 2% to GH¢17.67 per litre, while diesel could fall by 3.32% to GH¢19.30 per litre. LPG, however, is expected to rise by 18.5% to GH¢20.60 per kilogram. During the October 1 pricing window, most oil marketing companies maintained their prices following a GH¢2 levy on diesel and a government intervention in which Tema Oil Refinery and Sentuo Oil supplied refined products to the companies at previous prices. Reasons for the price changes The Chamber attributed the projected adjustments to developments on the international market and recent government subsidy measures. In its report, the Chamber said average crude oil prices rose by 2.03% to US$126.73 per barrel for the October 16 pricing window. It attributed the increase to renewed supply concerns, as Ukraine questioned a proposed US-backed energy ceasefire and Saudi Arabia faced fresh attacks amid the war with Iran. Prices of refined petroleum products, however, recorded mixed movements. LPG rose by 7.77%, while diesel fell by 6.68% and petrol declined by 3.93%. Meanwhile, the Ghana cedi depreciated by 1.61% to GH¢11.8222 to the US dollar, based on average bank rates between September 26 and October 11, 2026. The Chamber said the cedi had lost more than 11% against the dollar so far this year, with seasonal import demand and higher energy costs continuing to put pressure on the currency. Despite these developments, petrol and diesel prices are expected to see only modest reductions at the pumps, in line with projections from several analysts earlier this month. NPA lowers petrol and diesel price floors The National Petroleum Authority (NPA) has also reduced the minimum prices for petrol and diesel for the October 16 pricing window. Market data sighted by Joy Business shows that the petrol price floor has been lowered from GH¢16.45 to GH¢16.09 per litre. The diesel price floor has also been reduced from GH¢17.97 to GH¢17.09 per litre. The LPG price floor, however, has increased from GH¢11.10 to GH¢13.87 per kilogram. The NPA said these price floors exclude premiums charged by International Oil Trading Companies (IOTCs), operating margins of Bulk Import, Distribution and Export Companies (BIDECs), and margins charged by Oil Marketing Companies and LPG Marketing Companies. Those charges will be determined independently by the respective companies in accordance with the prescribed Petroleum Products Pricing Formula.

items.title: Makkah Alliance sec-gen meets PM Shehbaz, briefs premier on defence cooperation
items.description: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday met the newly appointed secretary-general of the Makkah Defence Alliance, Lieutenant General (retd) Nauman Mahmood, and was briefed on the strategy to promote “defence and strategic cooperation” under the pact, state-run Radio Pakistan reported. Lt Gen (retd) Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary general of the defence alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye last month. The agreement — signed on August 7 — empowers member states to treat an attack against one of them as an attack against all. During the meeting, the premier reiterated that the pact was a “historic milestone for peace, unity, and stability in the region” and wished Lt Gen (retd) Mahmood well for his new role. PM Shehbaz also reaffirmed Pakistan’s “unwavering commitment” to the protection of Saudi Arabia’s “sovereignty, territorial integrity and security” during the meeting as the Gulf state, which is a signatory to the pact, has faced escalating tensions with Yemen’s Houthi rebels in recent days. The premier said Pakistan “stands shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia, according to Radio Pakistan. The meeting comes amid heightened tensions in the Middle East. On Tuesday, Saudi Arabia launched strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, targeting fuel and energy facilities it said were being used to support missile and drone attacks, as the Yemeni group threatened a “harsh and painful” response against Saudi airports, refineries and oil installations. Hours later, Saudi authorities issued warnings of potential hostile aerial threats in the kingdom’s eastern province and Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard near Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, according to witnesses. Later, a Saudi energy ministry official confirmed the attack. Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency said that four people — two women, a man and a child — were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged. The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unravelled in July. Against this backdrop, Pakistan has repeatedly expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia. On October 5, in an emergency meeting of the Makkah pact in Riyadh, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye agreed to the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities. Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was part of Pakistan’s delegation in the meeting, maintained that Pakistan and Turkiye had “presence in theatre” and only Saudi troops were involved in combat operations. On September 18, Inter-Services Public Relations Director General Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Pakistan would go to “any extent” to defend the Gulf state, adding that Islamabad’s commitment to the kingdom’s security is “unconditional”. Asif has also reaffirmed that Pakistan will “practically and diplomatically” stand by Saudi Arabia against Yemen’s Houthi rebels if the situation escalates. The defence minister said that Pakistan would fulfil all its obligations under the Makkah Defence Alliance in accordance with the terms of the agreement between the three countries. At the same time, Pakistan has also asserted that the alliance is intended for collective deterrence and is defensive in nature.

items.title: Bank of Ghana engages stakeholders in Techiman
items.description: The Bank of Ghana (BoG) has held a day’s stakeholder engagement forum at Techiman in the Bono East Region, to strengthen stakeholder collaboration towards deepening public understanding of the mandate of the central bank and its policy development. The forum, the central bank said, further sought to maintain financial stability and to create value for money. It was on the theme: “Strengthening stakeholder relations through dialogue and engagement” and attended by traditional authorities, religious leaders, traders and market women, transport unions, Small and Medium Enterprises, community banks and microfinance institutions. The stakeholders were taken through the mandate of the BoG, as well as microfinance sector reforms, responsible borrowing and consumer protection, currency education and identification, and proper handling of banknotes among others. Addressing the stakeholders, Mr Bernard Otabil, the Director of Communications at the BoG, said the engagement was part of the BoG nationwide drive to deepen public understanding and to strengthen the nation’s financial sector. He explained that the engagement was designed to enable the BoG to access feedback from the public towards policy development and unlicensed financial schemes and currency abuses. Mr Otabil emphasised that the central bank remained dedicated to the public and strengthened public trust and confidence in the Ghana cedi. “The Cedi is not just a paper or coin, but it’s trust and we can’t formulate the best monetary policy, if the trader in Techiman market does not understand or trust the cedi,” he stated, adding: “That is why we are here, to listen, to dialogue, and to partner for financial reforms and stability.” Mr Otabil reiterated the BoG commitment to sustaining open dialogue with stakeholders across the regions and to promote financial literacy and financial inclusion. He urged members of the public to report suspected activities of unlicensed financial institutions to the bank. Mr Abdulai Lawal Abubakar, the Regional Director, Sunyani office of the BoG noted that the central bank remained committed to engaging stakeholders and to gather information that would foster the development of the bank. “Our engagement is meant to interact with and engage stakeholders to improve the total development of our operations that would enhance the BoG’s policy,” he added. Some of the stakeholders commended the central bank, describing the engagement as an eye opener and insightful. They expressed concern about high lending rates as well as activities of unregulated lenders and called on the BoG to do more to tackle those challenges.

items.title: Section 144 imposed in DI Khan, pillion riding and public gatherings banned
items.description: DERA ISMAIL KHAN: The district administration imposed Section 144 across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Dera Ismail Khan district, banning pillion riding and public gatherings, rallies and processions until Nov 11, citing law and order concerns. The restrictions were imposed through an order issued by Deputy Commissioner Hikmatullah on Oct 13 and took immediate effect. Under the order, public gatherings, meetings, processions and rallies that could potentially disturb public order, disrupt traffic or obstruct the movement of citizens have been prohibited. The administration has also imposed restrictions on the display of weapons and the installation of tents and temporary structures on public roads, according to the notification. The order said the measures had been taken in view of the prevailing law and order situation in the district. Those found violating the restrictions would face legal action under Section 188 of the Pakistan Penal Code, the administration warned. The restrictions will remain in force across the district until Nov 11, unless withdrawn or modified by the competent authority before that date. Section 144 is a provision in the Code of Criminal Procedure which empowers local authorities to ban public gatherings such as rallies, processions and sit-ins, as well as the open display of weapons. Currently, Section 144 remains in effect in several areas of the country. On Sunday, it was imposed in Karachi , set to remain in effect till Oct 20. On Saturday, Section 144 was imposed in Rawalpindi district for a period of 30 days. Punjab Home Department also imposed Section 144 across the province until Oct 15 in view of serious threats to public peace, tranquility and the safety of life and property.

items.title: PIAC unable to verify GH¢21m petroleum-funded projects in Ayawaso West
items.description: The Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC) has been unable to verify four petroleum revenue-funded projects valued at about GH¢21 million in the Ayawaso West Municipality because of inadequate information and vague project descriptions. ‎The projects could not be identified during a field inspection to assess the use of petroleum revenues between 2012 and 2024. ‎Mr Isaac Dwamena, Executive Secretary of PIAC, said the Committee had written to the Ministry of Roads and Highways three weeks before the inspection to request additional information but had not received a response by the time of the visit. ‎The inspection team, led by Nana Soglo Alloh IV, a PIAC member and Paramount Chief of the Likpe Traditional Area, identified three road projects and a Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compound with assistance from officials of the Assembly. ‎The road projects were the surfacing of Mega Link Road at Mempeasem, valued at GH¢178,170.13; construction of a 0.45-metre U-drain along Nii Sai Road, costing GH¢130,114.85; and surfacing of Nii Sai Road, valued at GH¢131,923.65. ‎The three projects were implemented by the Ministry of Special Initiatives. ‎The team also identified a CHPS compound at Mempeasem, which received GH¢657,395.99 in 2020 and was implemented by the Ministry of Health. ‎The four projects that remained unlocated included the construction of a concrete drain at East Legon, valued at GH¢3.35 million, and emergency road rehabilitation works costing GH¢3.9 million. ‎The rehabilitation works involved the upgrading of Spintex Road and roads and culverts in the East Legon area. ‎The other projects were the resealing of selected roads in Ayawaso West and Ga Central, valued at GH¢1.5 million, and the Boundary Road and Motorway Slip Road projects, estimated at GH¢12 million. ‎The projects were attributed to the Ministry of Water Resources, Works and Housing and the Ministry of Roads and Highways as implementing agencies. ‎Mr Dwamena said the information requested from the Ministry of Roads and Highways included the names and contact details of the contractors who executed the projects. ‎“When you go to the field armed with relevant information, it positions you better to carry out the exercise and get the results you want,” he said. ‎Mr Dwamena said PIAC could not conclude that the projects did not exist because it lacked the information needed to locate them. ‎“We would not say categorically that the projects do not exist. The information that would have enabled us to find the project, we didn’t get from the Ministry of Roads and Highways,” he said. ‎At a post-inspection meeting, Mr Gordon Domayele, Municipal Coordinating Director of the Ayawaso West Municipal Assembly, said information-sharing on centrally implemented projects was necessary to improve monitoring and accountability. ‎He called on the Central Government to involve the assemblies in projects undertaken within their jurisdictions. ‎“Sometimes, when people come from the national to ask certain questions, they think that some of us are not on top of the issue. It is not our fault,” he said. ‎The inspection formed part of PIAC’s mandate to collect data from stakeholder institutions and conduct physical visits to projects funded with petroleum revenues to assess value for money and promote transparency and accountability in the management of the revenues.

items.title: Ketu North MP led delegation petitions government over deteriorating Weta Irrigation Scheme
items.description: Eric Edem Agbana, Member of Parliament (MP) for Ketu North, has led a delegation of chiefs, rice farmers and concerned youth from Weta to petition the Ministry of Food and Agriculture for urgent rehabilitation of the deteriorating Weta Irrigation Scheme. The petition, presented on Monday, was received on behalf of the Minister by Mr John Dumelo, Deputy Minister of Food and Agriculture, who assured the delegation of the government’s commitment to rehabilitating the scheme and supporting farmers to revive the agricultural facility. The delegation called for immediate intervention to restore the irrigation infrastructure and reclaim farmlands severely damaged by years of operational challenges. The farmers said more than 1,200 families had been affected by the situation and appealed for appropriate compensation to help them recover their livelihoods. They also called for a thorough investigation into the utilisation of World Bank funds released for the redevelopment of the scheme to ensure accountability and transparency in the implementation of the project. Mr Agbana described the scheme as a critical agricultural asset with significant potential to boost rice production, create employment and strengthen Ghana’s food security. He said the continued deterioration of the facility had imposed considerable hardship on farmers and their families, stressing the need for urgent and decisive government intervention. The MP assured the delegation that he would continue to engage the relevant authorities to secure concrete action towards rehabilitating the scheme and addressing the concerns of affected farmers. He said the intervention should result in a clear rehabilitation plan, accountability for funds committed to the project and a credible strategy to restore the livelihoods of farmers. Mr Agbana reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the concerns of the people of Weta remained on the national agenda until meaningful progress was achieved.

items.title: Unpaid contractor delays KATH Mother and Baby Unit as materials deteriorate
items.description: The stalled Mother and Baby Unit project at the Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH) is facing further setbacks, with its consultant project manager warning that construction materials procured for the facility are deteriorating, and some have already become defective or expired due to prolonged delays. Consultant Project Manager Emmanuel Fobi Asabere disclosed this during a visit by Parliament’s Select Committee on Health to the abandoned facility in Kumasi to assess the project’s status and challenges. He said the contractor had been unable to resume full-scale construction because payments for work already undertaken remained outstanding, leading to repeated suspensions. Mr Asabere said the project had been suspended for about 14 months, following an earlier period of reduced activity due to payment delays. He explained that although the contractor had continued to maintain the site during the suspension, the prolonged inactivity was putting the procured materials and their warranty protections at risk. “The suspension is as a result of non-payment to the contractor,” he said, adding that the contractor was awaiting payment before returning to work. The project began in November 2019 as an effort to complete an existing hospital structure planned to accommodate about 850 beds. However, assessments conducted after the contractor took over revealed serious structural defects. Three other firms and the Ghana Institution of Engineers were subsequently engaged to evaluate the building, and their assessment concluded that repairing it would not be economically advisable. The project was therefore redesigned as a 509-bed hospital, involving the demolition of the old structure and construction of a new facility. Mr Asabere said the project initially cost €138.5M, but repeated suspensions led to additional expenses. He put physical construction progress at approximately 56 per cent and procurement at 75 per cent, while confirming that the design work and demolition of the previous structure had been completed. The outstanding payments, he warned, remain a major obstacle to resuming construction and completing the facility.

items.title: Kofi Adams says Ghanaians ignored warnings over World Cup visa payments
items.description: Minister for Sports and Recreation Kofi Adams says some Ghanaians disregarded repeated warnings against paying intermediaries who promised to secure United States and Canadian visas for the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with post-tournament information suggesting that money changed hands without the Ministry’s knowledge. He said prospective travellers had been cautioned against trusting individuals who claimed they could influence visa decisions through personal connections with government officials or members of the World Cup oversight committee. Mr Adams urged Ghanaians seeking travel assistance to use registered travel and tour companies with clear procedures and contractual obligations. He said some of the individuals allegedly demanded money by presenting themselves as friends of the Minister or people with access to the oversight committee. He warned that such claims should not be treated as a guarantee of visa approval, stressing that the Ministry had not authorised individuals to collect money on its behalf to influence visa applications. Speaking to Channel One TV on Tuesday, October 13, Mr Adams said he had issued several public warnings before the tournament. However, information gathered afterwards indicated that some people still paid intermediaries, including individuals allegedly holding official positions. “Before the World Cup, as Minister, on several occasions I had cause to warn Ghanaians and advise Ghanaians not to give money out to anybody in the name of going to offer you a visa to go to the US or Canada,” he said. The comments come amid scrutiny of alleged visa facilitation arrangements involving the Ghana Tourism Authority and the National Sports Authority. The Minority in Parliament has raised concerns over claims that some applicants were charged between US$7,000 and US$14,000 for visa assistance. President John Dramani Mahama has directed Yaw Ampofo Ankrah to step aside as Director-General of the National Sports Authority as police investigate the allegations.

items.title: Banks to charge 20% VAT on payments for Netflix, Zoom, TikTok and others
items.description: Commercial banks are preparing to apply 20 per cent Value Added Tax (VAT) to payments for cross-border digital services and e-commerce transactions made with cards issued in Ghana, according to information gathered by Joy Business. The banks say they are implementing a directive from the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA). However, Joy Business has yet to establish the details of the directive or whether any banks have already begun applying the tax. Standard Chartered Bank has notified its customers by email that it will begin applying the 20 per cent VAT to payments for cross-border digital services made with its Ghana-issued cards from October 15, 2026. According to the bank, the move is in line with GRA requirements. Transactions expected to be affected Information gathered by Joy Business suggests that the tax could cover payments across the following categories. The full scope and treatment of individual services are yet to be confirmed: Digital media and entertainment: Services such as Netflix, Spotify, Disney+, Showmax and beIN Sports. Software and software as a service: Products and subscriptions from Microsoft, Adobe, Zoom, Salesforce and Google Workspace. Cloud and hosting services: Platforms such as Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, DigitalOcean and SiteGround. Digital gaming and betting: Payments to platforms such as Steam, Blizzard, Roblox, DraftKings and Betway Ghana. Education and subscriptions: Services such as Coursera, Udemy, MasterClass and Cambridge University Press. Digital advertising: Payments for Google Ads, Meta Ads, TikTok Ads and LinkedIn advertising. Social media and communication: Paid services offered by platforms such as TikTok, LinkedIn, X and WhatsApp Business. Online travel and hospitality: Payments through platforms such as Booking.com, Agoda, Hotels.com, Uber and Bolt. Computer and IT services: Payments to providers such as Groundhog Tech and Neris Analytics. Security and VPN services: Subscriptions to services such as McAfee, NordVPN and ExpressVPN. What it means for customers Customers paying for affected services with debit or credit cards issued in Ghana should expect the 20 per cent VAT to be added to the amount payable. Some commercial banks have stressed that the additional cost is a tax imposed under GRA requirements, rather than a fee introduced by the banks. For affected transactions, customers could therefore pay the service price, the applicable VAT and any existing bank transaction charges.

items.title: Education Minister appeals to GAUA to call off strike, resume work on October 19
items.description: Haruna Iddrisu, the Minister of Education, has appealed to the leadership of the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA) to call off their strike and allow academic activities to resume at public universities by October 19, 2026. The Minister urged their leadership to return to the negotiation table with the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission (FWSC) to resolve the outstanding issues. “I will issue a directive to the Ghana Tertiary Education Commission by close of the week to request public universities to reopen by October 19, 2026,” the Minister announced at a meeting with the leadership of GAUA on Monday. He expressed the expectation that the striking workers – GAUA – would return to work by that date, subject to continued engagement on their outstanding concerns. The Minister said the strike had already affected the reopening schedules of the University of Ghana and the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, which had announced postponements of their reopening dates. He expressed the hope that the universities would reopen on October 19 to enable academic work to resume and prevent further disruption to the academic calendar. “I want to request GAUA to consider calling off the strike action for normal academic work to proceed and continue throughout all our university campuses across Ghana,” he said. The Minister clarified that his role in the discussions was to facilitate negotiations on behalf of the Government, explaining that salary negotiations fell outside the direct mandate of the Ministry of Education. He, however, acknowledged that the Government remained the employer of the affected workers and assured the unions that their legitimate concerns would receive priority attention. On issues that could be addressed immediately, the Minister said the Ministry would expedite action through the GTEC to request public universities extend the retirement rollover arrangement to all senior members, in line with previous practice. He disclosed that the Minister of Finance had issued a warrant for the payment of the one-off research allowance, adding that the relevant institutions were expected to complete the necessary administrative and payroll processes to facilitate payment. On the issue of market premium, the Minister said the matter, including the restoration of parity, had been referred to the FWSC for further engagement with the unions. He expressed optimism that the Commission would take the necessary action within its mandate and communicate the consequential steps required from the Ministry of Finance to address the unions’ concerns. The Minister recalled that the Minister of Finance had committed to a negotiated 40 per cent adjustment to the market premium and non-basic allowance, saying the Government considered that matter to have made progress towards resolution. He urged the union leaders to consult their members and reconsider the strike in the interest of students and the preservation of the academic calendar. The Minister said the Government’s efforts to align the reopening of schools at all levels in September were intended to improve the coordination of the country’s academic calendar, stressing that further disruptions could undermine that objective.

items.title: Mahama assures Assemblies of God of support for World Congress
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has assured the World Assemblies of God Fellowship of the Government’s continued support for the successful hosting of its World Congress in Accra. He gave the assurance when the Executive Committee of the Fellowship, led by Reverend Dominic Yeo, Global Chairman, and Reverend Stephen Wengam, General Superintendent of the Assemblies of God, Ghana, paid a courtesy call on him. The Congress, being held on African soil for the first time in the 115-year history of the Assemblies of God worldwide, is expected to bring together church leaders and members from across the globe. President Mahama welcomed the delegation to Ghana and pledged the Government’s commitment to ensuring that the event was peaceful, successful and impactful. Reflecting on his personal association with the Assemblies of God Church, the President said: “I have no regrets.” He commended the current leadership of the Church for its growth and transformation over the years. Rev Wengam said preparations for the Congress had been completed and expressed appreciation to President Mahama and the Government for their support in organising the event. He explained that the morning session of the Congress, originally scheduled to take place at the Independence Square, had been relocated to the Grand Arena of the Accra International Conference Centre due to technical challenges. According to him, the new venue offers a more conducive environment for the programme. Rev Yeo congratulated Ghana on becoming the first African country to host the World Congress, drawing a parallel with the nation’s historic status as the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to attain political independence. He expressed the Executive Committee’s gratitude to President Mahama and the Government for the support provided towards the successful organisation of the Congress. The Global Chairman also commended the President’s leadership, describing it as visionary and transformational, and cited economic stability and road infrastructure development as evidence of that leadership. He encouraged President Mahama to continue to represent Christ well in politics and remain steadfast in his faith. As part of the visit, Rev Yeo presented Congress souvenirs to the President and led the delegation in prayers for him and the prosperity of Ghana.

items.title: Ghana must prioritise home-grown AI solutions to meet national needs – UNDP
items.description: Ms Shaima Hussein, Deputy Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), has urged Ghana to prioritise locally developed artificial intelligence (AI) solutions that address national needs, strengthen public institutions and safeguard the country’s digital sovereignty. She said digital transformation efforts must focus on solutions that responded to Ghana’s development priorities rather than relying solely on technologies developed elsewhere. “What we need to support here is a local solution. And that’s actually the ultimate goal of our digital portfolio,” she said. Ms Hussein made the call at the opening of a three-day Digital and AI Champions Training for government officers selected from Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs), Monday in Accra. The training, organised by the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations in partnership with UNDP, with funding from the Government of Japan, is under the Accelerating Public Sector Digital Transformation through Capacity Building programme. The programme sought to equip public officials with the knowledge and skills to identify institutional challenges, adopt appropriate digital solutions and improve government efficiency. Ms Hussein said Ghana had established a strong foundation for digital transformation through initiatives such as the Ghana Card, interoperable payment systems and Ghana.gov, but needed to strengthen public institutions’ ability to use digital infrastructure, data and AI to improve service delivery. “We need to support local solutions, local systems, and systems that speak to the needs of the country and respect its sovereignty,” she said. She said responsible AI adoption required institutional capacity, effective data governance and ethical safeguards, adding that public officials must be equipped to assess AI solutions, protect public data and retain responsibility for decisions made using such technologies. The Digital and AI Champions Training, Ms Hussein would therefore help participants identify data gaps and institutional barriers within their respective ministries and determine where coordinated interventions could deliver the greatest impact. She said an AI accelerator component would provide a practical pathway for developing use cases by clarifying problems, assessing institutional readiness and risks, and designing responsible experiments. At the end of the training, Ms Hussein said the UNDP and the Ministry would convene a strategic dialogue to examine digital governance priorities and agree on next steps towards developing an integrated digital and AI portfolio across government. The initiative, she said, aimed to equip 50 government officers as certified Digital and AI Champions, while strengthening the capacity of 40 chief directors and 120 directors to commission, procure, govern and lead digital initiatives. Mr Emmanuel Ofori, Director of Innovations at the Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, urged public sector institutions to treat AI adoption as a strategic management and decision-making priority rather than the sole responsibility of information technology professionals. “AI is for decision making. It’s a decision making or decision support technology. It is not IT,” he said. Mr Ofori noted that Ghana had made significant progress in digital transformation through initiatives such as digital government services, national digital identification and interconnected mobile money services, which had helped improve access, efficiency and interactions between citizens and public institutions. However, he stressed that the next phase of the country’s digital transformation must move beyond individual technologies and isolated projects towards a more coordinated, problem-driven approach. He described the Digital Champions initiative as an important step towards building the capacity needed to accelerate public sector innovation. He, therefore, urged participants to identify operational bottlenecks, improve the use of data and explore how digital technologies could address challenges within their institutions. “The success of this programme will be measured by what changes because you were here. When you return to your respective institutions, I hope you will carry with you new perspectives, practical ideas and confidence to question processes that can be improved,” he added. Madam Izumi Kume, Coordinator for Economic Cooperation at the Embassy of Japan, said the training reflected Japan’s commitment to supporting Ghana’s digital transformation through capacity building and local ownership. She encouraged participants to apply the knowledge acquired to improve public administration and deliver better services to citizens.

items.title: Mahama truly cares – Obuobia Darko-Opoku
items.description: Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, the Administrator, Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF), has urged Ghanaians to always remember that President John Mahama feels their burden as his own and moves to act, not just sympathise. During the fourth stop of the Fund’s nationwide regional stakeholder engagement at Ho, she said the Fund was created to end the painful cycle where a single diagnosis like cancer, kidney disease, a cardiovascular condition, stroke or complications of diabetes threw an entire Ghanaian family into financial hardship. The GMTF, a national statutory fund established to mobilise sustainable financing for specialised medical care for people living with chronic Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs), is an initiative of President Mahama to provide financial support and specialised care for Ghanaians suffering from chronic NCDs not fully covered by the National Health Insurance Scheme. Positioned at the apex of Ghana’s three-tier health financing system, the GMTF, popularly known as “Mahama Cares” complements Free Primary Health Care (FPHC) and the NHIS by closing the critical financing gap for high-cost, specialised treatment that often falls beyond the routine NHIS coverage. Madam Darko-Opoku noted that the burden went beyond the patient, as relatives were forced to abandon work to provide care, children’s education disrupted, savings depleted and family assets sold to keep treatment going. “These are the circumstances that led the government to establish the Trust Fund,” she said. “In line with President Mahama’s vision, we have been entrusted with building an institution that supports eligible Ghanaians who require high-cost treatment for chronic non-communicable diseases and strengthens the healthcare system.” Madam Darko-Opoku explained that the Fund embarked on a nationwide assessment of teaching hospitals and major referral facilities to understand the real challenges in specialised care. The exercise showed that financial support alone would not be enough if diagnostic services remained weak, equipment inadequate and specialist numbers were limited. She said that engagement informed the Fund’s current operational four interconnected pillars – financial support for eligible patients, provision of medical equipment and infrastructure, specialist training and capacity development, and research and innovation. Touching on progress so far, the Administrator revealed that the Fund had piloted its systems with 50 patients nationwide, developed a medicines list and tariffs in collaboration with specialists, and operationalised the GMTF Care platform. She added that infrastructure interventions had begun, including the restoration of the cardiac catheterisation laboratory at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital and ongoing cardiology centre projects at Komfo Anokye and Tamale Teaching Hospitals to expand access to dialysis and other critical services. Madam Darko-Opoku commended Ho Teaching Hospital and the University of Health and Allied Sciences (UHAS) for their role in clinical care, training and research, describing them as essential partners. She appealed to traditional leaders, Members of Parliament, religious leaders, health professionals and the media to help carry accurate information about the Fund’s mandate, eligibility criteria and access processes to communities across the region. “Always remember and never forget that truly, Mahama Cares,” she emphasised. Prof Lydia Aziato, UHAS Vice-Chancellor who is an oncology nurse and passionate about breast cancer described the GMTF as an answered prayer, recalling a quote from a breast cancer patient, in those days when there was no one to talk to patients. Patients were just left alone with the diagnosis, and many resorted to faith and by the time they realised it was not a spiritual problem, the disease had advanced, creating huge burden in terms of cost of care, Prof Aziato added. She commended government for the three-tier health financing system, saying the FPHC would help detect these cases early and by the time they got to the hospitals the disease could be treated successfully and, in most cases, cured so the women could live their full years on earth. Prof. Aziato urged women to detect early, treat early because someone cared, and encouraged all who had the disease not to hide, but be bold and take advantage of the opportunity to seek medical care at the hospital.

items.title: Fire at GRIDCo Mallam substation disrupts power in parts of Accra
items.description: A fire outbreak at a substation operated by the Ghana Grid Company Limited (GRIDCo) at Mallam has disrupted electricity supply to parts of Accra, including Lapaz, Mallam and Awoshie. The blaze reportedly destroyed control boards and transformers at the facility, raising concerns about the impact on power transmission and electricity supply to affected communities. The extent of the damage and the time required to restore normal operations have not yet been confirmed. Firefighters from the Adjen Kotoku and Amasaman fire stations responded to the incident and worked to contain the blaze. Their intervention helped prevent the fire from spreading to other critical installations within the substation, limiting the potential damage to additional equipment. The cause of the outbreak remains unknown, with further investigations expected to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident. Technical assessments will also be needed to determine the full extent of the damage and the work required to restore affected installations. GRIDCo operates Ghana’s national electricity transmission network, transporting power from generation facilities to distribution companies for onward supply to consumers. Substations play a critical role in the system by housing transformers, control boards and other equipment used to regulate and manage electricity flows. Damage to these installations can complicate operations and delay the restoration of normal supply to affected areas.

items.title: Your client is Parliament, not a party; remain honest even when unwelcome – Speaker
items.description: Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, the Speaker of Parliament, has declared that the independence of parliamentary legal advice is not a technical detail but a democratic imperative. As a result, he has charged Legal Counsel to Parliaments across Africa that their ultimate loyalty was to Parliament as a constitutional institution and not to any political party or individual. Opening the 8th Africa Colloquium of Legal Counsel to Parliaments in Accra on Tuesday, he described legislative counsel and drafters as the quiet and indispensable architects of constitutional democracy. The Speaker made the remarks in a speech read his behalf by Reverend Ebenezer Ahumah Djietror, the Clerk to Parliament. He said politics was both a privilege and a profound institutional responsibility, and that they met not as isolated delegations, but as custodians of a shared constitutional aspiration and as joint architects of Africa’s democratic future. The Colloquium, hosted by the Parliament of Ghana from Monday, October 12 to Friday, October 16, 2026, on the theme: “Ethics, Integrity and Legal Accountability,” had brought together legal counsels from across the continent, to review 15 years of the Nairobi Principles. Speaking on impartiality, the Speaker said whether Parliament served the public or the powerful hinges on the independence of its legal advice: “Political eloquence alone has never built a durable nation, ordered national affairs or protected citizens from state overreach. That is where your work begins.” He stated that although parliamentary legal practice began with impartiality, it did not mean indifference. “It does not require counsel to feign neutrality or to pretend that all legal arguments are equally valid. It requires professional judgement without affection, ill-will, or partisan instruction,” he stated. Quoting the judicial oath to do right to all manner of people without fear or favour, affection or ill-will, he said that is the standard for parliamentary legal services. “Your advice must remain honest, even when it is unwelcome. A legal opinion that is welcomed by the majority may be correct. A legal opinion that frustrates the majority may also be correct. The test is not whether an advice pleases the institution at a particular moment, but it is whether it is legally written, professionally defensible, constitutionally sound and institutionally responsible,” he said. He was emphatic on where loyalty must lie, saying “Your professional loyalty must not be reduced to the interest of the majority party or the minority part, nor should it be understood as personal loyalty to an individual presiding officer. Your ultimate responsibility is to the institution of Parliament, the Constitution, and the public interest that Parliament exists to serve. In practical terms, your client is not a party nor a person. Your client is a constitutional institution,” he stressed. He said such responsibility required moral courage to tell leadership that a policy objective may be commendable, but the law had not been properly crafted. “Such advice is not disloyalty. It is the essence of constitutional responsibility,” he added. On Integrity, the Speaker said it was more than the absence of impropriety; it was fidelity to truth, law, duty and institutional purpose. He warned that Parliamentary counsel must resist the temptation to use legal reasoning to disguise political convenience, saying advice must not be shaped merely to produce the preferred answer. The Speaker further cautioned members against selectively commissioning legal opinions until a favourable conclusion was obtained, noting that where one opinion flagged serious risks on a fast-tracked Bill affecting fundamental rights and another indicated that the risk was manageable, presenting only the second opinion to leadership does not serve the law, but amounted to short-circuiting it. Touching on accountability and Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Speaker charged counsel to subject every Bill, amendment, application for constitutional validation, Private Member’s bill and subsidiary legislation to objective and analytically consistent scrutiny, regardless of political interest. “Every Bill drafted, every amendment written and every item of subsidiary legislation reviewed will have an encounter in the real world. In drafting, lack of precision creates ambiguity. In subsidiary legislation, absence of quality control means executive agencies may exercise powers Parliament never intended to confer,” he said. He explained that accountability meant being prepared to say in writing when a law was likely to be challenged, when delegation was too broad, or when procedure may not survive judicial review, and that parliamentary legal services themselves must be subject to codes of conduct, integrity training, annual reports, and transparent quality assurance. “We cannot demand accountability from the executive while insulating parliamentary legal services from legitimate institutional scrutiny,” he said. He warned that AI may assist in research and drafting but introduced risks of confidentiality breach, fabricated authorities, hidden biases, and weak audit trails. “Technology may accelerate the preparation of legislation, but it cannot determine whether the process is just, whether discretion is excessive or whether the legal framework will protect the vulnerable or empower the predator. That responsibility remains human,” he said. He therefore charged the Colloquium to adopt principles ensuring that no authority is drafted by AI that no human has reviewed; no draft is uploaded to insecure systems, and every use of AI can be audited. Proposing a forward agenda, the Speaker, urged delegates to strengthen respect for each country’s constitutional position, establish minimum standards on conflict of interest and confidentiality, institutionalise quality assurance through plain language drafting and post-legislative review, adopt a protocol for responsible AI use, and invest in continuous professional development. “You are guardians of constitutional boundaries, protectors of public resources and custodians of the legal processes through which citizenship can be lived with dignity and confidence,” he charged. “When you leave this court, let your measure not be how much was passed but how clearly it was written, how fairly it was processed and how justly it will operate,” he added. Dr Dominic Akuritinga Ayine, the Attorney-General and Minister for Justice, urged Legal Counsel to Parliaments across Africa to use the ongoing 8th Africa Colloquium to develop practical protocols on the use of AI and the handling of improper instructions. “I urge you to take advantage of these days to share how our respective offices handle improper instructions, work towards a practical protocol for the use of AI in legislative work, give the principles a measurable self-assessment and strengthen training and mentorship for the next generation of legislative counsel,” he said. He charged delegates to take the answers home to their respective Parliaments to make them responsive to the needs of citizens across the continent. He thanked counsel for their service to various Parliaments, including the support being provided to the Parliament of the Republic of Ghana. Mr Alexander Kwamena Afenyo-Markin, the Minority leader, said professional integrity demands that parliamentary lawyers refuse to draft legislation inconsistent with constitutional requirements. He said it also requires advising the Speaker and Committee Chairs with candour and intellectual honesty, even when that advice goes against the ambitions of influential political actors. “Professional integrity requires resistance to attempts to manipulate parliamentary procedures to marginalise minority voices, restrict legitimate scrutiny or suppress dissent,” he said. Mr Afenyo-Markin cited Principle Eight of the Nairobi Principles, which requires parliamentary legal offices to remain impartial and non-partisan. He stressed that non-partisanship must not be confused with neutrality, explaining that it entails a principled commitment to procedural justice. “The Constitution and the Standing Orders guarantee minority rights to ask questions, participate in debate, examine evidence and propose amendments. Parliamentary counsel has a responsibility to ensure that parliamentary majorities do not extinguish democratic fairness,” he stated. He said the 15-year review of the Nairobi Principles should not be an exercise in institutional self-congratulation but a rigorous, honest and fearless self-assessment. “We must ask ourselves deeper questions: In how many of our parliaments are legal counsel genuinely autonomous? Where has executive influence gradually reasserted itself to weaken parliamentary legal offices? Where are counsel being marginalised, under-resourced or denied the institutional authority necessary to fulfil their mandate?” he queried. He told delegates that as they return to their respective capitals, they carry the expectations of millions of African citizens who regard Parliament as the final institutional bulwark against authoritarianism, corruption, arbitrariness and abuse of power. “Be independent, be ethical, be courageous. Our parliaments will endure only on the foundations of integrity, constitutionality and accountability,” he said. Mr James Agalga, the Majority Leader, said good governance rests on certainty, institutional stability and fidelity to law. “Government programmes can endure only when their legislation is grounded in constitutional principle and sound legal principle. Legislation arising from complex reforms, fiscal policy or bilateral investment agreements must not receive uncritical approval or superficial scrutiny,” he said. He said what the majority requires and what the national interest demands is a parliamentary counsel capable of subjecting legislation to rigorous technical scrutiny, identifying constitutional vulnerabilities candidly, and improving legislative language to withstand judicial scrutiny. “Your foremost obligation is to the law, the Constitution and the integrity of the legislature,” he charged counsel. He said rigorous legal analysis during committee considerations does not obstruct government policy but rather strengthens it by identifying legal and constitutional risks, thereby preventing procedural invalidation, unnecessary litigation and constitutional uncertainty. Reflecting on the Nairobi Principles established 15 years ago in 2011, when parliaments assembled in Nairobi articulated a far-sighted vision for Africa’s parliaments to develop autonomous, professional and ethical in-house legal expertise, he commended the progress made across the continent. “From regional assemblies to national parliaments and county legislatures, the office of parliamentary legal counsel has evolved from an experimental administrative reform into an indispensable institution for legislative governance,” he said. On the theme of the Colloquium, “Ethics, Integrity and Legal Accountability”, he said it touches the very foundations of responsible statecraft at a time of rapid socio-economic transformation, heightened public expectations and complex international realities. “Ethical integrity cannot be treated as an abstract idea. It anchors public confidence and democratic legitimacy,” he added.

items.title: Mahama urges chiefs to help tackle galamsey, protect water bodies
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has appealed to traditional authorities to intensify their support for the government’s fight against illegal mining, warning that community resistance and the lack of alternative livelihoods continue to undermine efforts to curb the menace. He made the appeal when he received a delegation from the Western North Regional House of Chiefs at the Presidency in Accra. The delegation, led by Ogyeahoho Yaw Gyebi II, was at the Presidency to congratulate the President on his victory in the 2024 elections, acknowledge development projects in the region and present concerns requiring government attention. Mr Mahama said enforcement operations had uncovered senior high school students working at illegal mining sites because their families could not afford to support their education. He disclosed that several young people had been arrested, with hundreds awaiting trial, but argued that law enforcement must be accompanied by economic opportunities. “Alongside enforcing the law against illegal mining, we must provide alternative livelihoods. That is why we are implementing the New Economy Policy,” he said, adding that investment in job-creating sectors, including tourism, could help steer young people away from galamsey. The President also called for stronger community cooperation with the National Inter-Ministerial Coordinating Committee on Illegal Mining (NAIMOS), particularly in forest reserves and around water bodies. He said resistance from some community members and traditional authorities had resulted in dangerous confrontations with security personnel, including incidents involving gunfire and fatalities. The President further announced that the government had allocated an additional GH¢400 million in the next Budget to recruit more Blue Water Guards to patrol water bodies and destroy changfang machines encountered during operations. Mr Mahama said the government had cleared all nine forest reserves previously classified as red zones because of extensive destruction and the presence of heavily armed illegal miners. He added that soldiers had been stationed in the areas to prevent miners from returning after earlier operations were followed by renewed incursions. The government, he said, was also working with the military and Forestry Commission through GoldBod-supported efforts to reclaim degraded land, level damaged sites and replant economic trees. Ogyeahoho Gyebi commended the President for development projects in the region and reaffirmed the chiefs’ commitment to supporting efforts to promote peace and national development. Mr Mahama reiterated that traditional authorities were essential partners in the fight against illegal mining because of their close ties to local communities and their ability to help build support for enforcement and alternative livelihood programmes.

Bank of Ghana pilots digital cross-border payments with Rwanda, Nigeria
items.description: The Bank of Ghana is testing cross-border interoperability using central bank digital currencies, stablecoins, bank accounts and mobile wallets. This is being implemented in the corridors between Rwanda and Nigeria. The pilots in the two corridors have been designed to test whether different forms of money can move seamlessly across borders without passing through correspondent banks outside the continent. The central bank has also extended the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System, (PAPSS) to mobile wallets in the Ghana–Nigeria corridor, marking a shift from bank-only settlement to inclusion of mobile money. Dr Johnson Pandit Asiama, the Governor, Bank of Ghana, made the disclosure at a high-level event on the margins of the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Group (WBG) annual meetings in Bangkok on Tuesday. The event was on the theme: “Digital innovations in payments; SSA future Agenda,” on the back of the continent moving beyond adoption to scaling digital payments that delivered efficiency, inclusion and stability across the region. “The Bank is testing cross-border interoperability using CBDCs, stablecoins, bank accounts and mobile wallets in the Ghana–Rwanda and Ghana–Nigeria corridors and has extended PAPSS to mobile wallets in the Ghana–Nigeria corridor,” Dr Asiama said. He explained that the objective was to move the pilots to live services, building on existing infrastructure such as PAPSS rather than creating new systems, with the interoperability testing to meet users where they already transacted. He said bringing mobile wallets onto PAPSS could allow a trader in Accra to pay a supplier in Lagos instantly in local currency, without needing a dollar intermediary or a foreign correspondent bank. The Central Bank Governor said with mobile wallets were dominant in both Ghana and Nigeria, and Rwanda becoming a key partner for regulatory innovation, the partnership between Ghana, Rwanda and Nigeria was strategically important. He stated that until now, PAPSS largely operated a bank-to-bank system, limiting its reach to customers who are already banked, while most cross-border trade was driven by mobile money users. The new approach, he said, reflected a growing consensus among African central banks that interoperability, not new infrastructure, was the key to reducing costs and improving speed and transparency. “The future of African payments will not be defined by a single technology, and central banks should not determine which technology succeeds. Our role is to ensure that emerging systems are safe, efficient, resilient and inclusive,” Dr Asiama said. He called for enhanced regional collaboration to build a safe, efficient, and inclusive payment ecosystem that supports Africa’s trade, investment, and long-term development ambitions. On regulation, the Central Bank Governor raised concerns over African fintechs facing costly and duplicative licensing in each market they entered, even where the activities and risks were similar. “Our Licence Passporting Framework with the National Bank of Rwanda offers a practical model, and we are engaging more than 10 countries to join. We would welcome its adoption as a regional approach, alongside common standards for payment messaging, payee verification, and fraud data sharing,” he said.

Cedi edges higher as GoldBod boosts dollar supply to banks
items.description: The Ghana cedi has recorded marginal gains against the US dollar on the interbank market for the second consecutive week, supported by improved foreign exchange liquidity. Market watchers estimate the appreciation at just under 1%, offering some relief after sustained pressure on the local currency since the third quarter. The pressure has been linked to increased demand for dollars by businesses financing imports ahead of December, as well as energy-related payments by the Bank of Ghana for crude oil and finished petroleum products. The recent gains follow near-weekly depreciation since last month. What is driving the recovery? Market players have attributed the recovery to increased foreign exchange support, particularly dollar sales by the Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod). On Tuesday, GoldBod sold US$197 million to commercial banks at a rate of GH¢11.70 to the dollar. Joy Business understands that every participating bank received the full amount it requested, easing demand pressures and raising expectations of further gains for the cedi. The sales, conducted through GoldBod’s GoFX platform, complement other measures by the Bank of Ghana to support liquidity in the foreign exchange market. The intervention is in line with GoldBod’s plan to supply US$1 billion to commercial banks under its revised arrangements for foreign exchange receipts from gold exports in the artisanal and small-scale mining sector. Some commercial banks have told Joy Business that they expect the cedi to remain fairly stable if the improved liquidity support is sustained.

items.title: Le siège houthiste de Taïz menace le gouvernement yéménite
items.description: Taïz, la troisième ville la plus peuplée du Yémen, située à environ 140 kilomètres au nord-ouest d’Aden, est désormais entièrement encerclée par les Houthis, qui ont pris le contrôle des principales voies d’approvisionnement Fear strikes Yemen’s 3rd largest city Taiz as Houthi rebels encircle it in a new siege », Associated Press , 13 octobre 2026.'> 1 . La ville était déjà largement coupée des zones tenues par le gouvernement depuis le 6 octobre. Taïz occupe une position de pivot entre le nord-ouest du pays, contrôlé par les Houthis, et le sud, contrôlé par le gouvernement. Cela fait plusieurs années que le groupe cherche à s’emparer de la ville, qu’il a assiégée de 2015 à 2024 sans jamais parvenir à la prendre. Malgré la contre-offensive menée par les forces gouvernementales avec l’appui de l’Arabie saoudite, les Houthis continuent de progresser et leur poussée pourrait affaiblir la position d’Aden le long de la côte de la mer Rouge, en particulier autour de Dhubab. Selon les données cartographiques de l’Institute for the Study of War, analysées par la revue, les Houthis auraient étendu de plus de 2 500 km² le territoire qu’ils contrôlent autour de Taïz entre le 16 septembre et le 12 octobre. Cette progression rapide suggère que la contre-offensive lancée par le gouvernement et l’Arabie saoudite au début du mois n’a pas permis, à ce stade, d’enrayer l’avancée du groupe. En effet, les moyens engagés par Riyad semblent insuffisants pour infliger des pertes significatives au groupe. Le royaume craint par ailleurs une escalade qui risquerait de plonger le pays dans un conflit long et coûteux. Les Houthis ont frappé à deux reprises l’aéroport de Riyad les 10 et 11 octobre, provoquant au moins 14 morts et plusieurs centaines de blessés. La première de ces attaques a été la plus meurtrière en Arabie saoudite depuis plus d’une décennie. Selon une source diplomatique, Israël aurait proposé à Riyad de rejoindre la campagne contre les Houthis, ce que le prince héritier Mohammed ben Salmane aurait refusé, craignant la réaction de l’opinion publique Netanyahu Seeks Saudi Arabia's Approval to Join Fight Against Houthis, but Crown Prince Opposes Move », Haaretz , 12 octobre 2026.'> 2 . Plusieurs pays, dont la France, le Royaume-Uni, le Pakistan et la Turquie, ont renforcé leur présence militaire en Arabie saoudite ou annoncé l’envoi de matériel défensif depuis l’intensification des attaques houthistes, en septembre. Les États-Unis fournissent quant à eux des services de renseignement et une aide au ciblage à l’armée saoudienne, et ont déployé une batterie Patriot supplémentaire. L’article Le siège houthiste de Taïz menace le gouvernement yéménite est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Court acquits Sharjeel Memon in liquor case
items.description: KARACHI: After eight years, a judicial magistrate on Tuesday acquitted Senior Sindh Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon and five others in a case pertaining to the recovery of liquor from his Dr Ziauddin Hospital room. The then chief justice of Pakistan, Mian Saqib Nisar, had raided the room and allegedly found the liquor. Later, a case was registered at the Boat Basin police station under Section 4 (owning or possessing intoxicant) of the Prevention (enforcement of Hadd) Ordinance 1979 read with Section 201 (causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen offender) and 34 (common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code. On Tuesday, after hearing and examining the records, Judicial Magist­rate (South) Aasim Aslam acquitted Mr Memon and five others for lack of evidence against them. In its order, the court observed that the prosecution alleged that the suspected liquor bottles were recovered from the possession of the accused persons. However, the chemical examination report of the recovered bottles does not support the prosecution allegations. Rather, it mentioned that the bottles contain honey and olive oil. “Thus, both the reports being material pieces of evidence have failed to corroborate the prosecution version. It is settled principle of criminal jurisprudence that the prosecution is bound to establish the case beyond the reasonable doubt and the burden of proving the guilt of accused cannot be shifted upon him,” the court observed. It added that mere allegations of the police officials in the absence of reliable and corroborative evidence were insufficient to sustain a conviction particularly when the scientific evidence available on record contradicts the prosecution story. The judge also noted that the prosecution case in these circumstances has failed to establish the essential ingredients of the alleged offences beyond a reasonable doubt. According to the prosecution, on Sept 1, 2018, the then assistant superintendent of Karachi Central Prison received information that illegal activities were taking place in a private hospital room where Mr Memon was staying due to illness. The room had been declared a sub-jail as Mr Memon was in judicial custody in connection with a NAB reference. The prosecution added that jail police went to the room and recovered two bottles, one allegedly containing alcohol and the other apparently containing honey. Later, a case was registered against Mr Memon and his employees at the Boat Basin police station. During the trial, defence counsel Uroosha Memon argued before the court that Mr Memon was falsely implicated in the case for political victimisation. She further argued that as per chemical reports the alleged bottles contained honey and olive oil, adding that despite it being a crowded place, the police did not associate any private witness. Published in Dawn, October 14th, 2026

items.title: Judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, Politico amid legal fight
items.description: A federal judge extended access to the White House for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists, ruling on Tuesday that President Donald Trump likely broke the law when he tried to ban them, in the latest ruling against him in the press freedom dispute. US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a written decision elaborating on his September 24 emergency order reinstating access for the journalists. The news organisations and press freedom groups have accused Trump of unconstitutional retaliation against journalists for coverage he does not ​like. Kelly’s order last month gave CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists temporary access to the White House grounds. The judge ​issued a preliminary injunction on Tuesday that will remain in effect until he issues a final judgment in the lawsuit brought by the news organisations, unless an appeals court lifts it. Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against ​the media has been unprecedented. He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their ​reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to the administration. He has also filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets. Trump announced the ban in September on his social media platform, saying those news organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.” The Justice Department has emphasised Trump’s ​contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds. The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for ​their news coverage and accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban. The outlets said in a lawsuit that the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment by the government. The White House on September 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after the judge decided the ban “likely violated their constitutional due process rights,” and ordered their access immediately restored. The judge, who Trump appointed in 2017 during his first presidential term, also raised doubts about the US Justice Department’s national security arguments to justify the ban, noting that Trump himself had said the action was due to what the president alleged was false or negative coverage. Justice Department lawyers have said the outlets endangered national security by publishing classified information, citing stories about US missile stockpiles, construction of Trump’s White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican ​midterm convention. ‘COERCE BETTER COVERAGE’ The judge held a hearing on October 8 to hear arguments from the news outlets and the Justice Department over whether to extend protection for journalists against being barred from the White House. The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified. “Here we have the unusual situation where the president himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wants to coerce better coverage,” Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told ⁠Kelly during ​the hearing. “CNN, MS NOW and Politico engaged in apparently indefensible conduct,” Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik ​said. The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the November 3 US midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings are ​at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war.

items.title: DGSN : 33 morts dans 2.424 accidents en une semaine en périmètre urbain
items.description: La Direction générale de la sûreté nationale (DGSN), a fait savoir que 33 personnes ont trouvé la mort et 3.153 autres ont été blessées, dont 132 grièvement, dans 2.424 accidents de la circulation survenus en périmètre urbain durant la semaine allant du 05 au 11 octobre. Ces accidents, précise la DGSN, sont principalement dus, dans l’ordre, à l’inadvertance des conducteurs, au non-respect de la priorité, à l’excès de vitesse, à l’inadvertance des piétons, au non-respect de la distance de sécurité, à la non maîtrise du véhicule, au changement de direction sans usage du clignotant, au changement de direction non autorisé, au non-respect du stop, à la circulation en sens interdit, à la circulation sur la voie gauche, au non-respect du feu rouge, à la conduite en état d’ébriété et au dépassement défectueux. Concernant les opérations de contrôle et de répression en matière de circulation, les services de sûreté ont enregistré 52.026 contraventions, dressé 8.097 procès-verbaux transmis au Parquet et procédé au recouvrement de 43.929 amendes transactionnelles, selon la même source. Les sommes perçues au titre de ces contraventions ont atteint 9.634.800 dirhams, ajoute le communiqué, faisant état de la mise en fourrière municipale de 5.333 véhicules, de la saisie de 8.097 documents et du retrait de la circulation de 625 véhicules.
